arXiv:2403.03667v2 [quant-ph] 18 Jul 2024

Random covariant quantum channels

Ion Nechita Email address: nechita@irsamc.ups-tlse.fr Address: Laboratoire de Physique Théorique, Université de Toulouse, CNRS, UPS, France and Sang-Jun Park Email address: spark@irsamc.ups-tlse.fr Address: Laboratoire de Physique Théorique, Université de Toulouse, CNRS, UPS, France
Abstract.

The group symmetries inherent in quantum channels often make them tractable and applicable to various problems in quantum information theory. In this paper, we introduce natural probability distributions for covariant quantum channels. Specifically, this is achieved through the application of “twirling operations” on random quantum channels derived from the Stinespring representation that use Haar-distributed random isometries. We explore various types of group symmetries, including unitary and orthogonal covariance, hyperoctahedral covariance, diagonal orthogonal covariance (DOC), and analyze their properties related to quantum entanglement based on the model parameters. In particular, we discuss the threshold phenomenon for positive partial transpose and entanglement breaking properties, comparing thresholds among different classes of random covariant channels. Finally, we contribute to the PPT2 conjecture by showing that the composition between two random DOC channels is generically entanglement breaking.

1. Introduction

Quantum channels are essential mathematical constructs in quantum theory, modeling the most general evolution open quantum systems can undergo. Generalizing the unitary quantum dynamics described by Schrödinger’s equation, quantum channels have been studied extensively, from different perspectives [NC10, Wil17, Wat18]. In physics, quantum channels describe the evolution of quantum states as they propagate through space and/or time, and model usually the noise coming from the environment. In quantum information theory, quantum channels model the transmission of quantum information between distant parties, akin to a classical communication channel but with quantum properties. Mathematically, quantum channels are represented by completely positive, trace preserving maps.

The study of covariant quantum evolutions was initiated by Holevo [Hol93, Hol96]. This type of covariance encodes usually a symmetry present in the system Hamiltonian and can be mathematically formulated as follows:

∀g∈G,Φ⁡(πA​(g)⋅πA​(g)∗)=πB​(g)​Φ​(⋅)​πB​(g)∗.\forall g\in G,\qquad\Phi\Big(\pi_{A}(g)\cdot\pi_{A}(g)^{*}\Big)=\pi_{B}(g)\Phi(\cdot)\pi_{B}(g)^{*}.

Above, πA\pi_{A} and πB\pi_{B} are unitary representations of the physical symmetry group GG. A channel Φ:ℳd​(ℂ)→ℳd​(ℂ)\Phi:\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) having the property above is called a (πA,πB)(\pi_{A},\pi_{B})-covariant channel. This notion is not only important in physically-relevant settings where symmetry is present, but also as a tool in several areas of quantum information theory, such as quantum cloning [KW99], programmability [GBW21], quantum Shannon theory [WH02, Kin03, Hol05, DHS06, KW09, DTW16, WTB17, BCLY20], etc. The importance of this notion stems also from the fact that group symmetries inherent in quantum channels often make them tractable and applicable to various problems in quantum information theory, especially related to quantum entanglement [VW01, COS18, CMHW18, siudzinska2018quantum, BCS20, SN21, SN22b, PJPY23, PY23]. Their general structure and mathematical properties have been extensively studied in recent years [AN14, MSD17, MS22, LY22].

Another way to probe the structure of quantum channels is to consider their generic behavior, that is to study random quantum channels. Broadly speaking, random quantum channels model typical behavior of quantum operations [BCSŻ09], hence it is of crucial importance to understand their physical and mathematical properties, such as: entanglement, information transmission capacity, spectral properties, etc. A systematic study of the different models of random quantum channels and of their properties can be found in [KNP+21a]. Moreover, random constructions for quantum channels have played a crucial role in many areas of quantum Shannon theory, mainly as a source of (counter-)examples [HW08, Has09, BCN16, CN15, CP22]; this situation is parallel to classical information theory, where random constructions of codes and channels are ubiquitous.

In this work, we consider random covariant quantum channels. We introduce and study probability distributions on the set of covariant quantum channels, for different choices of group symmetry. We find in which asymptotic regimes such channels are PPT or entanglement breaking. In particular, we explain the threshold phenomenon for these two properties. We show that in the case of diagonal symmetry, random covariant channels satisfy the PPT2 conjecture. Our work sets up the framework for the study of random covariant channels, by defining the relevant probabilistic models in the most common settings of group symmetry. We expect the models and the results in this paper to find further applications in quantum information theory, in the study of problems having a specific type of symmetry and also as a rich source of examples of channels with a tractable form.

We shall consider several cases of (random) covariant channels, corresponding to the standard representations of:

  • •

    the unitary group 𝒰d={U∈ℳd​(ℂ):U∗​U=Id}\mathcal{U}_{d}=\{U\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\,:\,U^{*}U=I_{d}\}

  • •

    the orthogonal group 𝒪d={U∈ℳd​(ℝ):O⊤​O=Id}\mathcal{O}_{d}=\{U\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{R})\,:\,O^{\top}O=I_{d}\}

  • •

    the hyperoctahedral group ℋd={±1}≀𝒮d\mathcal{H}_{d}=\{\pm 1\}\wr\mathcal{S}_{d} of signed permutation matrices

  • •

    the diagonal unitary group 𝒟𝒰d={diag(ei​θ1,…,ei​θd):θ1,…,θd∈ℝ}\mathcal{DU}_{d}=\{\operatorname{diag}(e^{\mathrm{i}\theta_{1}},\ldots,e^{\mathrm{i}\theta_{d}})\,:\,\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{d}\in\mathbb{R}\}

  • •

    the diagonal orthogonal group 𝒟𝒪d={diag(ε1…,εd):ε1,…,εd=±1}\mathcal{DO}_{d}=\{\operatorname{diag}(\varepsilon_{1}\ldots,\varepsilon_{d})\,:\,\varepsilon_{1},\ldots,\varepsilon_{d}=\pm 1\}.

We depict in Fig. 1 the groups (left) and the corresponding classes of covariant channels (right). Edges correspond to set inclusion relations, meaning that the source is contained in the target. Top elements correspond to the largest groups (reps. channel sets), while bottom elements correspond to the smallest groups (resp. channel sets). The notation is self-evident, with the exception of (see Section 5):

DUC channels ↔(𝒟𝒰d×𝒟𝒰d) covariance\displaystyle\quad\leftrightarrow\quad(\mathcal{DU}_{d}\times\mathcal{DU}_{d})\text{ covariance}
CDUC channels ↔(𝒟𝒰d×𝒟​𝒰¯d) covariance\displaystyle\quad\leftrightarrow\quad(\mathcal{DU}_{d}\times\overline{\mathcal{DU}}_{d})\text{ covariance}
DOC channels ↔(𝒟𝒪d×𝒟𝒪d) covariance.\displaystyle\quad\leftrightarrow\quad(\mathcal{DO}_{d}\times\mathcal{DO}_{d})\text{ covariance}.

The contributions of our work are two-fold:

  • •

    Entanglement theory: we find the range of parameters ss for which random covariant channels are asymptotically PPT, respectively EB. In particular, we specify the threshold s0s_{0} such that, in the limit d→∞d\to\infty, the probability that random covariant channels are PPT/EB tends to 11 (resp. <1<1) whenever whenever s≫s0s\gg s_{0} (resp. s≪s0s\ll s_{0}).

  • •

    PPT2 conjecture: we generalize the main result of [SN22b]. Furthermore, we show that random DOC channels satisfy the PPT2 conjecture, under very general conditions.

We recall that a quantum channel is PPT (positive partial transpose) if the composition of the channel with the (non-physical) transpose map is still a quantum channel. On the other hand, a quantum channel is called entanglement breaking (EB) if, when applied to one system of a bipartite quantum state, the output bipartite state is separable [HSR03]. Our results on the PPT and EB properties of random covariant tables are informally presented in the table below. The rows of the table are ordered, starting with the largest groups on the top, and finishing with the smallest group at the bottom. The last row of the table corresponds to no symmetry whatsoever, hence to random channels before the twirling operation. Here s0s_{0} denotes the threshold for corresponding properties. For example, s0∼const.s_{0}\sim\text{const.} for PPT means that we have the property with probability 11 (resp. <1<1) whenever d→∞d\to\infty and s=s⁡(d)→∞s=s(d)\to\infty (resp. ss is fixed). Note that the two last columns are devoted to the entanglement breaking (EB) property of channels: since deciding whether a channels is EB is an 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-hard problem, it is difficult in general to obtain sharp thresholds for this property. All the results present in the table are new, with the exception of the last row.

We present below the statement of a formal result, corresponding to the CDUC, DUC, and DOC rows of the table above; see Theorems 5.10 and 5.13 for the details.

Let Φ𝖣𝖴𝖢∼μd,s𝖣𝖴𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{DUC}}\sim\mu^{\mathsf{DUC}}_{d,s}, Φ𝖢𝖣𝖴𝖢∼μd,s𝖢𝖣𝖴𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{CDUC}}\sim\mu^{\mathsf{CDUC}}_{d,s}, and Φ𝖣𝖮𝖢∼μd,s𝖣𝖮𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{DOC}}\sim\mu^{\mathsf{DOC}}_{d,s} be, respectively, random DUC, CDUC, and DOC channels. Then:

    In the regime s/d→0s/d\to 0, Φ𝖢𝖣𝖴𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{CDUC}} and Φ𝖣𝖮𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{DOC}} are almost surely not PPT as d→∞d\to\infty.

Note that in item (5) above we show that the smallest eigenvalue of the partial transpose of the Choi matrix of the random channels we consider converges to a positive value. We also obtain results about the realignment criterion [CW03, Rud05] applied to the Choi matrix of DUC, CDUC, and DOC channels in Proposition 5.12.

Our second contribution concerns the PPT2 conjecture for DOC channels. Motivated by the theory of quantum repeaters, this conjecture [Chr12, CMHW18] has received a lot of attention in the recent years. The conjecture states that the composition of two arbitrary PPT quantum channels is entanglement breaking. Recent works establish the conjecture in several restricted scenarios, or with weaker conclusions [LG15, KMP17, RJP18, CMHW18, CYT19, HRF20, GKS20, JY20, SN22b]. Moreover, in the case of random quantum channels (without any covariance property), it has been proven [CYZ18] that two independent random quantum channels that are PPT satisfy the conjecture.

Regarding the quantum channels with diagonal orthogonal symmetry, it has been shown in [SN22b] that the PPT2 conjecture holds for any two DUC / CDUC channels, while the same question for DOC channels has been left open. We tackle this question from both deterministic and random perspectives. The results can be summarized as follows; see Corollaries 6.4 and 6.5 for the details.

Theorem B.
  1. (1)

    The PPT2 conjecture holds for the composition between any DOC and (C)DUC channels. That is, if Φ1,Φ2:ℳd​(ℂ)→ℳd​(ℂ)\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2}:\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) are two PPT channels such that Φ1\Phi_{1} is DOC and Φ2\Phi_{2} is DUC or CDUC, then both Φ1∘Φ2\Phi_{1}\circ\Phi_{2} and Φ2∘Φ1\Phi_{2}\circ\Phi_{1} are entanglement breaking.

  2. (2)

    Consider two random DOC channels Φi∼μd,si𝖣𝖮𝖢\Phi_{i}\sim\mu^{\mathsf{DOC}}_{d,s_{i}}, i=1,2i=1,2, in the asymptotic regime where d→∞d\to\infty and si≳dtis_{i}\gtrsim d^{t_{i}} for some constants ti>0t_{i}>0. Then, almost surely as d→∞d\to\infty, the composition Φ1∘Φ2\Phi_{1}\circ\Phi_{2} is entanglement breaking. In particular, in the asymptotic regime above, any two random DOC channels satisfy the PPT2 conjecture.

Note that Theorem B (1) generalizes the main result of [SN22b] by allowing one of the channels to belong to the larger class of DOC channels. Moreover, it is worth mentioning that the hypotheses of Theorem B (2) are very weak when compared to those of [CYZ18]: the channels need not be PPT, nor independent.

Our paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we recall the theory of covariant quantum channels and that of random quantum channels; we also give the general recipe for sampling random covariant quantum channels. Sections 3, 4 and 5 deal, respectively, with the three main classes of symmetry groups: unitary/orthogonal, hyperoctahedral, and diagonal unitary/orthogonal. These sections present the general structure theorems for the corresponding covariant channels, and then gather our main results regarding the PPT and EB properties of the random covariant quantum channels. Finally, Section 6 contains our result about DOC channels satisfying the PPT2 conjecture.

2. Random covariant quantum channels

In this section we recall two of the fundamental notions discussed in this paper: that of symmetric (covariant) quantum channels, and that of random quantum channels. In the rest of the paper, we shall combine these two points of view by analyzing the properties of random covariant quantum channels.

2.1. Covariant quantum channels

For a compact group GG, consider (finite-dimensional) unitary representations π:G→𝒰d\pi:G\to\mathcal{U}_{d}, πA:G→𝒰dA\pi_{A}:G\to\mathcal{U}_{d_{A}}, and πB:G→𝒰dB\pi_{B}:G\to\mathcal{U}_{d_{B}} of GG. Then we call

  1. (1)

    a matrix X∈ℳd​(ℂ)X\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) π\pi-invariant if π⁡(x)​X​π​(x)∗=X\pi(x)X\pi(x)^{*}=X for all x∈Gx\in G,

  2. (2)

    a linear map Φ:ℳdA​(ℂ)→ℳdB​(ℂ)\Phi:\mathcal{M}_{d_{A}}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d_{B}}(\mathbb{C}) (πA,πB)(\pi_{A},\pi_{B})-covariant if Φ⁡(πA​(x)​Z​πA​(x)∗)=πB​(x)​Φ​(Z)​πB​(x)∗\Phi(\pi_{A}(x)Z\pi_{A}(x)^{*})=\pi_{B}(x)\Phi(Z)\pi_{B}(x)^{*} for all x∈Gx\in G and Z∈ℳdA​(ℂ)Z\in\mathcal{M}_{d_{A}}(\mathbb{C}).

Let us denote by Inv⁡(π){\rm Inv}(\pi) (resp. Cov⁡(πA,πB){\rm Cov}(\pi_{A},\pi_{B})) the set of all π\pi-invariant matrices (resp. (πA,πB)(\pi_{A},\pi_{B})-covariant linear maps). π\pi is called irreducible if Inv⁡(π)=ℂ​Id{\rm Inv}(\pi)=\mathbb{C}I_{d} (which coincides with usual definition of irreducibility in representation theory, thanks to Schur’s lemma). If π\pi is irreducible, so is the contragredient representation π¯:G→𝒰d\overline{\pi}:G\to\mathcal{U}_{d} of π\pi which is defined by π¯​(x)=π⁡(x)¯\overline{\pi}(x)=\overline{\pi(x)} for x∈Gx\in G. For unitary representations πA:G→𝒰dA\pi_{A}:G\rightarrow\mathcal{U}_{d_{A}} and πB:G→𝒰dB\pi_{B}:G\rightarrow\mathcal{U}_{d_{B}}, the direct sum representation πA⊕πB:G→𝒰dA+dB\pi_{A}\oplus\pi_{B}:G\to\mathcal{U}_{d_{A}+d_{B}} (resp. tensor representation πA⊗πB:G→𝒰dA​dB\pi_{A}\otimes\pi_{B}:G\rightarrow\mathcal{U}_{d_{A}d_{B}}) is given by (πA⊕πB)​(x)=πA​(x)⊕πB​(x)(\pi_{A}\oplus\pi_{B})(x)=\pi_{A}(x)\oplus\pi_{B}(x) (resp. (πA⊗πB)​(x)=πA​(x)⊗πB​(x)(\pi_{A}\otimes\pi_{B})(x)=\pi_{A}(x)\otimes\pi_{B}(x)) for x∈Gx\in G. Two unitary representations π1:G→𝒰d1\pi_{1}:G\to\mathcal{U}_{d_{1}} and π2:G→𝒰d2\pi_{2}:G\to\mathcal{U}_{d_{2}} are said to be unitarily equivalent if there exists a unitary matrix U:ℂd1→ℂd2U:\mathbb{C}^{d_{1}}\to\mathbb{C}^{d_{2}} such that π2​(x)=U​π1​(x)​U∗\pi_{2}(x)=U\pi_{1}(x)U^{*} for all x∈Gx\in G, where we denote by π1≅π2\pi_{1}\cong\pi_{2}.

The following is a well-known fact in representation theory.

Proposition 2.1 ([Sim95]).

Suppose that a unitary representation π:G→𝒰d\pi:G\rightarrow\mathcal{U}_{d} has an irreducible decomposition of the form

(1) π≅⨁i=1lσi⊗Imi,\pi\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^{l}\sigma_{i}\otimes I_{m_{i}},

where σi:G→𝒰ni\sigma_{i}:G\to\mathcal{U}_{n_{i}} (i=1,2,…,li=1,2,\ldots,l) are mutually inequivalent irreducible sub-representations of π\pi with multiplicity mim_{i}, respectively. Then we have

(2) Inv⁡(π)≅⨁i=1lIni⊗ℳmi​(ℂ)⊆ℳni​(ℂ)⊗ℳmi​(ℂ).{\rm Inv}(\pi)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^{l}I_{n_{i}}\otimes\mathcal{M}_{m_{i}}(\mathbb{C})\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{n_{i}}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathcal{M}_{m_{i}}(\mathbb{C}).

In this section, we are interested in two types of twirling operations: for unitary representations π,πA,πB\pi,\pi_{A},\pi_{B} of GG,

  1. (1)

    π\pi-twirling 𝒯π​X:=𝔼G​[Adπ⁡(⋅)​(X)]=𝔼G​[π⁡(⋅)​X​π​(⋅)∗]\mathcal{T}_{\pi}X:=\mathbb{E}_{G}[{\rm Ad}_{\pi(\cdot)}(X)]=\mathbb{E}_{G}[\pi(\cdot)X\pi(\cdot)^{*}] for a matrix X∈ℳd​(ℂ)X\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}),

  2. (2)

    (πA,πB)(\pi_{A},\pi_{B})-twirling 𝒯πA,πB​Φ:=𝔼G​[AdπB​(⋅)∗∘Φ∘AdπA​(⋅)]\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{A},\pi_{B}}\Phi:=\mathbb{E}_{G}[{\rm Ad}_{\pi_{B}(\cdot)^{*}}\circ\Phi\circ{\rm Ad}_{\pi_{A}(\cdot)}] for a linear map Φ:ℳdA​(ℂ)→ℳdB​(ℂ)\Phi:\mathcal{M}_{d_{A}}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d_{B}}(\mathbb{C}),

where AdU:Z↦U​Z​U∗{\rm Ad}_{U}:Z\mapsto UZU^{*} and the expectation is defined with respect to the (normalized) Haar measure of the compact group GG.

Let us collect some useful properties of the twirling operations for the next section. First of all, 𝒯π\mathcal{T}_{\pi} is a conditional expectation onto the ∗*-subalgebra Inv⁡(π){\rm Inv}(\pi) of ℳd​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}). Note that for any (finite-dimensional) von Neumann subalgebra ℳ\mathcal{M} of ℳd​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}), there is a unique TP conditional expectation of ℳd​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) onto ℳ\mathcal{M} [BO08, Lemma 1.5.11]. For example, the map X∈ℳn​(ℂ)⊗ℳm​(ℂ)↦1n​In⊗Trn​(X)X\in\mathcal{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathcal{M}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\mapsto\frac{1}{n}I_{n}\otimes{\rm Tr}_{n}(X) is the unique TP conditional expectation onto ℳ=In⊗ℳm​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}=I_{n}\otimes\mathcal{M}_{m}(\mathbb{C}). This observation allow us to get the following explicit formula of the twirling map 𝒯π\mathcal{T}_{\pi} for the case ℳ=Inv⁡(π)\mathcal{M}={\rm Inv}(\pi).

Proposition 2.2.

In Proposition 2.1, let Πi\Pi_{i} be the orthogonal projection from ℂd\mathbb{C}^{d} onto ℂni⊗ℂmi\mathbb{C}^{n_{i}}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{m_{i}}. Then the twirling 𝒯π​(X)\mathcal{T}_{\pi}(X) of X∈ℳd​(ℂ)X\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) is given by

(3) 𝒯π​(X)=⨁i=1l1ni​Ini⊗Trni​(Πi​X​Πi).\mathcal{T}_{\pi}(X)=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{l}\frac{1}{n_{i}}I_{n_{i}}\otimes{\rm Tr}_{n_{i}}(\Pi_{i}X\Pi_{i}).

In particular, if the irreducible decomposition of π\pi is multiplicity-free, i.e., if mi≡1m_{i}\equiv 1 for all i=1,2,⋯,li=1,2,\cdots,l, then

(4) 𝒯π​(X)=∑i=1lTr⁡(Πi​X)ni​Πi.\mathcal{T}_{\pi}(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{l}\frac{{\rm Tr}(\Pi_{i}X)}{n_{i}}\Pi_{i}.
Proposition 2.3.

Let π0,π1:G→𝒰d\pi_{0},\pi_{1}:G\to\mathcal{U}_{d} be two unitary representations of GG such that Ran​π1⊂Ran​π0{\rm Ran\,}\pi_{1}\subset{\rm Ran\,}\pi_{0}. Then

𝒯π0∘𝒯π1=𝒯π1∘𝒯π0=𝒯π0.\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{0}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{1}}=\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{1}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{0}}=\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{0}}.
Proof.

Recall that each 𝒯πi\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{i}} is a TP conditional expectation onto Inv⁡(πi){\rm Inv}(\pi_{i}). Since Inv⁡(π0)⊂Inv⁡(π1){\rm Inv}(\pi_{0})\subset{\rm Inv}(\pi_{1}), we obviously have 𝒯π1∘𝒯π0=𝒯π0\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{1}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{0}}=\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{0}}. Next, observe that

(𝒯π0∘𝒯π1)∘(𝒯π0∘𝒯π1)=𝒯π0∘(𝒯π1∘𝒯π0)∘𝒯π1=𝒯π0∘𝒯π1∘𝒯π1=𝒯π0∘𝒯π1.(\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{0}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{1}})\circ(\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{0}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{1}})=\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{0}}\circ(\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{1}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{0}})\circ\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{1}}=\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{0}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{1}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{1}}=\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{0}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{1}}.

Since 𝒯π0∘𝒯π1\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{0}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{1}} is a unital CPTP map and Ran⁡(𝒯π0∘𝒯π1)=Inv⁡(π0){\rm Ran}(\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{0}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{1}})={\rm Inv}(\pi_{0}), 𝒯π0∘𝒯π1\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{0}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{1}} is a TP conditional expectation onto Inv⁡(π0){\rm Inv}(\pi_{0}). By the uniqueness, we conclude that 𝒯π0∘𝒯π1=𝒯π0\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{0}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{1}}=\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{0}}. ∎

Recall that the (unnormalized) Choi-Jamiołkowski matrix J⁡(Φ)J(\Phi) of a linear map Φ:ℳdA​(ℂ)→ℳdB​(ℂ)\Phi:\mathcal{M}_{d_{A}}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d_{B}}(\mathbb{C}) is defined by

(5) J⁡(Φ):=dA​[Φ⊗id]​(|ΩdA⟩⟨ΩdA|)=∑i,j=1dAΦ⁡(|i⟩​⟨j|)⊗|i⟩​⟨j|∈ℳdB​(ℂ)⊗ℳdA​(ℂ),J(\Phi):=d_{A}[\Phi\otimes\mathrm{id}](\outerproduct{\Omega_{d_A}}{\Omega_{d_A}})=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d_{A}}\Phi(|i\rangle\langle j|)\otimes|i\rangle\langle j|\in\mathcal{M}_{d_{B}}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathcal{M}_{d_{A}}(\mathbb{C}),

where |Ωd⟩\ket{\Omega_{d}} is the maximally entangled state

(6) |Ωd⟩:=1d​∑i=1d|i​i⟩∈ℂd⊗ℂd,\ket{\Omega_{d}}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\ket{ii}\in\mathbb{C}^{d}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{d},

and, for future reference, FdF_{d} is the flip (or swap) unitary operator

(7) Fd:=∑i,j=1d|i​j⟩⟨j​i|∈𝒰d2.F_{d}:=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}\outerproduct{ij}{ji}\in\mathcal{U}_{d^{2}}.

Importantly, the PPT and entanglement breaking (EB) properties of a channel can be read on its Choi matrix:

Φ​ is PPT\displaystyle\Phi\text{ is PPT } ⇔J⁡(Φ)​ is PPT\displaystyle\iff J(\Phi)\text{ is PPT}
Φ​ is EB\displaystyle\Phi\text{ is EB } ⇔J⁡(Φ)​ is separable.\displaystyle\iff J(\Phi)\text{ is separable.}

We recall that a positive semidefinite matrix X∈ℳdA​(ℂ)⊗ℳdB​(ℂ)X\in\mathcal{M}_{d_{A}}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathcal{M}_{d_{B}}(\mathbb{C}) is called

PPT  if XΓ=[id⊗⊤](X)≥0\displaystyle\quad\text{ if }\quad X^{\Gamma}=[\mathrm{id}\otimes\top](X)\geq 0
separable  if X=∑iAi⊗Bifor positive semidefinite matrices ​Ai∈ℳdA​(ℂ),Bi∈ℳdB​(ℂ).\displaystyle\quad\text{ if }\quad X=\sum_{i}A_{i}\otimes B_{i}\quad\text{for positive semidefinite matrices }A_{i}\in\mathcal{M}_{d_{A}}(\mathbb{C}),\,B_{i}\in\mathcal{M}_{d_{B}}(\mathbb{C}).

The following Proposition 2.4 establishes the connection between group symmetries of quantum channels and those of their Choi matrices.

Proposition 2.4 ([PJPY23]).

Let πA:G→𝒰dA\pi_{A}:G\to\mathcal{U}_{d_{A}} and πB:G→𝒰dB\pi_{B}:G\to\mathcal{U}_{d_{B}} be unitary representations of GG. Then, for any linear map Φ:ℳdA​(ℂ)→ℳdB​(ℂ)\Phi:\mathcal{M}_{d_{A}}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d_{B}}(\mathbb{C}),

J⁡(𝒯πA,πB​Φ)=𝒯πB⊗πA¯​(J⁡(Φ)).J(\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{A},\pi_{B}}\Phi)=\mathcal{T}_{{\pi_{B}}\otimes\overline{\pi_{A}}}\left(J(\Phi)\right).

In particular, Φ∈Cov⁡(πA,πB)\Phi\in{\rm Cov}(\pi_{A},\pi_{B}) if and only if J⁡(Φ)∈Inv⁡(πB⊗πA¯)J(\Phi)\in{\rm Inv}(\pi_{B}\otimes\overline{\pi_{A}}). Moreover, if Φ\Phi is PPT / EB, then so is 𝒯πA,πB​Φ\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{A},\pi_{B}}\Phi.

2.2. Random quantum channels

We shall now endow the set of all quantum channels with a probability measure, laying down the foundation for the study of symmetric (covariant) channels in the subsequent sections. The set of quantum channels (i.e. completely positive, trace preserving maps) Φ:ℳd​(ℂ)→ℳd​(ℂ)\Phi:\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) is a compact convex subset of the set of linear maps ℳd​(ℂ)→ℳd​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}). Actually, since quantum channels preserve Hermitian matrices, one can see it as a subset of hermiticity preserving maps ℳds​a​(ℂ)→ℳds​a​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}^{sa}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}^{sa}_{d}(\mathbb{C}). The trace preservation condition adds a number of linear restrictions, easily seen in the Choi-Jamiołkowski picture from Eq. (5): a linear map Φ\Phi is trace preserving iff

[Tr⊗id]​(J⁡(Φ))=Id.[\Tr\otimes\mathrm{id}](J(\Phi))=I_{d}.

Let VV be a Haar-distributed random isometry of size d​s×dds\times d and define the random Stinespring channel ΦV:ℳd​(ℂ)→ℳd​(ℂ)\Phi_{V}:\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) by

(8) ΦV​(ρ):=(idd⊗Trs)​(V​ρ​V∗).\Phi_{V}(\rho):=(\mathrm{id}_{d}\otimes{\rm Tr}_{s})(V\rho V^{*}).

The probability distribution of ΦV\Phi_{V} depends on the choice of dimension parameters dd and ss, and we shall denote it by μd,s\mu_{d,s}. Let us recall that a Haar-distributed random isometry V:ℂd→ℂd​sV:\mathbb{C}^{d}\to\mathbb{C}^{ds} can be obtained by truncating a random Haar-distributed unitary matrix U∈𝒰d​sU\in\mathcal{U}_{ds}.

According to [KNP+21b], we can give an equivalent definition for a random Stinespring channel ΦV\Phi_{V}. We first consider a random Wishart matrix W=G​G∗W=GG^{*} of parameter (d2,s)(d^{2},s) and set H:=(Trd⊗idd)​WH:=(\Tr_{d}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{d})W. Then HH is almost surely invertible, and the probability distribution of J⁡(ΦV)J(\Phi_{V}) is the same as that of

(9) J~:=(Id⊗H−1/2)W(Id⊗H−1/2).\tilde{J}:=(I_{d}\otimes H^{-1/2})W(I_{d}\otimes H^{-1/2}).

Note that the matrix J~\tilde{J} is PPT (resp. separable) if and only if WW is PPT (resp. separable). We gather below some of the foundational results from [Aub12, ASY14, CYZ18]. In our work, we shall prove similar results in the case of covariant channels.

Proposition 2.5.

Consider the random Stinespring channel Φd,s\Phi_{d,s} with parameter (d,s)(d,s).

  1. (1)

    (Threshold phenomenon of PPT property for Φ\Phi) For any ε>0\varepsilon>0

    • •

      if s<(4−ε)​d2s<(4-\varepsilon)d^{2}, limd→∞ℙ⁡(Φd,s​ is PPT)=0\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi_{d,s}\text{ is PPT})=0,

    • •

      if s>(4+ε)​d2s>(4+\varepsilon)d^{2}, limd→∞ℙ⁡(Φd,s​ is PPT)=1\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi_{d,s}\text{ is PPT})=1.

  2. (2)

    (Threshold phenomenon of EB property for Φ\Phi) There exist constants C1,C2>0C_{1},C_{2}>0 and a sequence sds_{d} satisfying

    C1​d3≤sd≤C2​d3​(log⁡d)2C_{1}d^{3}\leq s_{d}\leq C_{2}d^{3}(\log d)^{2}

    such that for any ε>0\varepsilon>0,

    • •

      if s<(1−ε)​sds<(1-\varepsilon)s_{d}, limd→∞ℙ⁡(Φd,s​ is EB)=0\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi_{d,s}\text{ is EB})=0,

    • •

      if s>(1+ε)​sds>(1+\varepsilon)s_{d}, limd→∞ℙ⁡(Φd,s​ is EB)=1\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi_{d,s}\text{ is EB})=1.

  3. (3)

    (4+ε)​d2<s<(1−ε)​sd(4+\varepsilon)d^{2}<s<(1-\varepsilon)s_{d}

    so that Φd,s\Phi_{d,s} and Φ~d,s\widetilde{\Phi}_{d,s} are generically PPT and not EB, then limd→∞ℙ⁡(Φd,s∘Φ~d,s​ is EB)=1\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi_{d,s}\circ\widetilde{\Phi}_{d,s}\text{ is EB})=1.

Let us end this introductory section by providing the general recipe that shall be used to produce random covariant channels in the following sections:

  1. (1)

    first, we sample a random quantum channel ΦV\Phi_{V}, without any symmetry, from the ensemble μd,s\mu_{d,s}, see (8)

  2. (2)

    we then symmetrize Φ\Phi using the twirling operation below, to obtain a random (πA,πB)(\pi_{A},\pi_{B})-covariant channel ΦπA,πB\Phi_{\pi_{A},\pi_{B}}:

    (10) ΦπA,πB​(X):=𝒯πA,πB​(ΦV)​(X)=∫GπB​(g)∗​ΦV​(πA​(g)​X​πA​(g)∗)​πB​(g)​𝑑𝔥​(g),\Phi_{\pi_{A},\pi_{B}}(X):=\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{A},\pi_{B}}(\Phi_{V})(X)=\int_{G}\pi_{B}(g)^{*}\Phi_{V}\Big(\pi_{A}(g)X\pi_{A}(g)^{*}\Big)\pi_{B}(g)\,\mathrm{d}\mathfrak{h}(g),

    where 𝔥\mathfrak{h} is the Haar measure on the group GG.

3. Random orthogonal covariant channels

In this section we study three basic and important classes of linear maps in quantum information theory, those having a unitary or orthogonal covariance group. Unitary covariance is a very strong form of symmetry, since input states can be diagonalized, the effect of the unitary rotation being transferred to the output of the channel. Such strong symmetry makes very suitable for analysis in various settings related to quantum Shannon theory. We recall below their definition.

  1. (1)

    The depolarizing maps characterized by (U,U)(U,U)-covariance:

    Φ⁡(U​Z​U∗)=U​Φ​(Z)​U∗,Z∈ℳd​(ℂ),U∈𝒰d,\Phi(UZU^{*})=U\Phi(Z)U^{*},\;\;Z\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}),\;U\in\mathcal{U}_{d},
  2. (2)

    The transpose depolarizing maps characterized by (U,U¯)(U,\overline{U})-covariance:

    Φ⁡(U​Z​U∗)=U¯​Φ​(Z)​U⊤,Z∈ℳd​(ℂ),U∈𝒰d,\Phi(UZU^{*})=\overline{U}\Phi(Z)U^{\top},\;\;Z\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}),\;U\in\mathcal{U}_{d},
  3. (3)

    The orthogonal covariant maps characterized by (O,O)(O,O)-covariance:

    Φ⁡(O​Z​O⊤)=O​Φ​(Z)​O⊤,Z∈ℳd​(ℂ),O∈𝒪d,\Phi(OZO^{\top})=O\Phi(Z)O^{\top},\;\;Z\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}),\;O\in\mathcal{O}_{d},
Proposition 3.1.

Let Φ:ℳd​(ℂ)→ℳd​(ℂ)\Phi:\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) be a quantum channel. Then, the (U,U)(U,U), (U,U¯)(U,\overline{U}), (O,O)(O,O) twirlings of Φ\Phi are given, respectively, by:

𝒯U,U​(Φ)\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{U,U}(\Phi) =p⋅id+(1−p)⋅Δ\displaystyle=p\cdot\mathrm{id}+(1-p)\cdot\Delta
(11) 𝒯U,U¯​(Φ)\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{U,\overline{U}}(\Phi) =q⋅⊤+(1−q)⋅Δ\displaystyle=q\cdot\top+(1-q)\cdot\Delta
𝒯O,O​(Φ)\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{O,O}(\Phi) =p′⋅id+q′⋅⊤+(1−p′−q′)⋅Δ,\displaystyle=p^{\prime}\cdot\mathrm{id}+q^{\prime}\cdot\top+(1-p^{\prime}-q^{\prime})\cdot\Delta,

where id,⊤,Δ\mathrm{id},\top,\Delta are, respectively, the identity, the transposition, and the completely depolarizing linear maps. Here the coefficients p,q,p′,q′p,q,p^{\prime},q^{\prime} are explicitly related to Φ\Phi by

p\displaystyle p =λ1−1d2−1,\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda_{1}-1}{d^{2}-1},
q\displaystyle q =λ2−1d2−1,\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda_{2}-1}{d^{2}-1},
p′\displaystyle p^{\prime} =(d+1)​λ1−λ2−dd​(d+2)​(d−1),\displaystyle=\frac{(d+1)\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}-d}{d(d+2)(d-1)},
q′\displaystyle q^{\prime} =(d+1)​λ2−λ1−dd​(d+2)​(d−1),\displaystyle=\frac{(d+1)\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{1}-d}{d(d+2)(d-1)},

where the parameters λ1,2\lambda_{1,2} associated to the channel are defined (see also Figure 2):

λ1​(Φ)\displaystyle\lambda_{1}(\Phi) :=d⁡⟨Ωd|J⁡(Φ)|Ωd⟩\displaystyle:=d\langle\Omega_{d}|J(\Phi)|\Omega_{d}\rangle
λ2​(Φ)\displaystyle\lambda_{2}(\Phi) :=Tr⁡(J⁡(Φ)​Fd).\displaystyle:=\Tr(J(\Phi)F_d).

Above we have used maximally entangled state |Ωd⟩\ket{\Omega_{d}} and the flip operator FdF_{d} defined respectively in Eq. 6 and Eq. 7.

Proof.

All the formulas follow from Proposition 2.2. Regarding the (U,U)(U,U)-twirling 𝒯U,U\mathcal{T}_{U,U}, note that the representation U∈𝒰d↦U⊗U¯U\in\mathcal{U}_{d}\mapsto U\otimes\overline{U} can be decomposed into two irreducible sub-representations whose corresponding projections are

|Ωd⟩​⟨Ωd|,Id2−|Ωd⟩​⟨Ωd|.|\Omega_{d}\rangle\langle\Omega_{d}|,\quad I_{d^{2}}-|\Omega_{d}\rangle\langle\Omega_{d}|.

Therefore, Proposition 2.2 and 2.4 implies that

J⁡(𝒯U,U​Φ)\displaystyle J(\mathcal{T}_{U,U}\Phi) =𝒯U⊗U¯​(J​(Φ))\displaystyle=\mathcal{T}_{U\otimes\overline{U}}(J(\Phi))
=Tr⁡(|Ωd⟩​⟨Ωd|​J​(Φ))⁡|Ωd⟩​⟨Ωd|+Tr⁡((Id2−|Ωd⟩​⟨Ωd|)​J​(Φ))​Id2−|Ωd⟩​⟨Ωd|d2−1\displaystyle=\Tr(|\Om_d\ra\la\Om_d|J(\Phi))|\Omega_{d}\rangle\langle\Omega_{d}|+\Tr((I_{d^2}-|\Om_d\ra\la\Om_d|)J(\Phi))\frac{I_{d^{2}}-|\Omega_{d}\rangle\langle\Omega_{d}|}{d^{2}-1}
=λ1d​|Ωd⟩​⟨Ωd|+(d−λ1d)​Id2−|Ωd⟩​⟨Ωd|d2−1\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda_{1}}{d}|\Omega_{d}\rangle\langle\Omega_{d}|+\left(d-\frac{\lambda_{1}}{d}\right)\frac{I_{d^{2}}-|\Omega_{d}\rangle\langle\Omega_{d}|}{d^{2}-1}
=λ1−1d2−1​d​|Ωd⟩​⟨Ωd|+d2−λ1d2−1​Id2d,\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda_{1}-1}{d^{2}-1}d|\Omega_{d}\rangle\langle\Omega_{d}|+\frac{d^{2}-\lambda_{1}}{d^{2}-1}\frac{I_{d^{2}}}{d},

where we used Tr⁡(J⁡(Φ))=d\Tr(J(\Phi))=d since Φ\Phi is TP. Therefore, we have the formula 𝒯U,U​(Φ)\mathcal{T}_{U,U}(\Phi) as in Eq. 11.

The remaining formulas can be derived analogously by noting that the representations U∈𝒰d↦U⊗UU\in\mathcal{U}_{d}\mapsto U\otimes U and O∈𝒪d↦O⊗OO\in\mathcal{O}_{d}\mapsto O\otimes O have the irrep decompositions corresponding to the projections (see [TiB16, Appendix A] and [Bra37])

Πsym:=Id2+Fd2,Πanti:=Id2−Fd2,\Pi_{\rm sym}:=\frac{I_{d^{2}}+F_{d}}{2},\quad\Pi_{\rm anti}:=\frac{I_{d^{2}}-F_{d}}{2},

and

|Ωd⟩​⟨Ωd|,Πsym−|Ωd⟩​⟨Ωd|,Πanti,|\Omega_{d}\rangle\langle\Omega_{d}|,\quad\Pi_{\rm sym}-|\Omega_{d}\rangle\langle\Omega_{d}|,\quad\Pi_{\rm anti},

respectively. ∎

The channel parameters λ1,2​(Φ)\lambda_{1,2}(\Phi) can take values in specific intervals, as follows.

Proposition 3.2.

For a channel Φ:ℳd​(ℂ)→ℳd​(ℂ)\Phi:\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}), we have

0≤\displaystyle 0\leq λ1​(Φ)≤d2\displaystyle\lambda_{1}(\Phi)\leq d^{2}
−d≤\displaystyle-d\leq λ2​(Φ)≤d,\displaystyle\lambda_{2}(\Phi)\leq d,

with the inequalities being tight.

Proof.

The map Φ↦𝒯U,U​(Φ)\Phi\mapsto\mathcal{T}_{U,U}(\Phi) is onto the set of channels of the form p⋅id+(1−p)⋅Δp\cdot\mathrm{id}+(1-p)\cdot\Delta. The range of pp for which the latter maps are quantum channels is known to be

p∈[−1d2−1,1],p\in\Big[\frac{-1}{d^{2}-1},1\Big],

hence the claim for λ1​(Φ)\lambda_{1}(\Phi) follows. The second claim can be proven in a similar manner, since the allowed range of qq is

q∈[−1d−1,1d+1].q\in\Big[\frac{-1}{d-1},\frac{1}{d+1}\Big].

∎

The PPT and entanglement breaking properties of (conjugate) unitary and orthogonal covariant channels are fully characterized by the parameters λ1,2​(Φ)\lambda_{1,2}(\Phi), as follows.

Proposition 3.3 ([VW01]).

For the parameters λ1​(Φ)\lambda_{1}(\Phi) and λ2​(Φ)\lambda_{2}(\Phi) defined above,

  1. (1)

    𝒯U,U​(Φ)\mathcal{T}_{U,U}(\Phi) is PPT iff it is EB iff 0≤λ1​(Φ)≤d0\leq\lambda_{1}(\Phi)\leq d;

  2. (2)

    𝒯U,U¯​(Φ)\mathcal{T}_{U,\overline{U}}(\Phi) is PPT iff it is EB iff 0≤λ2​(Φ)≤d0\leq\lambda_{2}(\Phi)\leq d;

  3. (3)

    𝒯O,O​(Φ)\mathcal{T}_{O,O}(\Phi) is PPT iff it is EB iff 0≤λ1​(Φ),λ2​(Φ)≤d0\leq\lambda_{1}(\Phi),\lambda_{2}(\Phi)\leq d.

We define now random covariant quantum channels by twirling the random quantum channels introduced in Section 2.2. More precisely, we introduce the following image distributions:

μd,sU,U\displaystyle\mu^{U,U}_{d,s} :=(𝒯U,U)#​μd,s\displaystyle:=(\mathcal{T}_{U,U})_{\#}\mu_{d,s}
μd,sU,U¯\displaystyle\mu^{U,\overline{U}}_{d,s} :=(𝒯U,U¯)#​μd,s\displaystyle:=(\mathcal{T}_{U,\overline{U}})_{\#}\mu_{d,s}
μd,sO,O\displaystyle\mu^{O,O}_{d,s} :=(𝒯O,O)#​μd,s.\displaystyle:=(\mathcal{T}_{O,O})_{\#}\mu_{d,s}.

Recall that μd,s\mu_{d,s} is the probability distribution of the random channel ΦV\Phi_{V} associated to the Haar random isometry V:ℂd→ℂd⊗ℂsV:\mathbb{C}^{d}\to\mathbb{C}^{d}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{s}. The distributions above are characterized by the parameters p,q,p′,q′p,q,p^{\prime},q^{\prime} from Proposition 3.1. In turn, these are related to the isometry VV defining the channel Φ\Phi via the following quantities:

λ1(d,s)\displaystyle\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)} :=λ1​(ΦV)=d⁡⟨Ωd|J⁡(ΦV)|Ωd⟩\displaystyle:=\lambda_{1}(\Phi_{V})=d\langle\Omega_{d}|J(\Phi_{V})|\Omega_{d}\rangle
λ2(d,s)\displaystyle\lambda_{2}^{(d,s)} :=λ2​(ΦV)=Tr⁡(J⁡(ΦV)​Fd),\displaystyle:=\lambda_{2}(\Phi_{V})=\Tr(J(\Phi_V)F_d),

see Figure 3 for a graphical representations of these scalars. Above, the random channel ΦV\Phi_{V} is defined via the Stinespring dilation from the Haar-distributed random isometry V:ℂd→ℂd⊗ℂsV:\mathbb{C}^{d}\to\mathbb{C}^{d}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{s}:

ΦV​(ρ)=Trs​[V​ρ​V∗].\Phi_{V}(\rho)=\Tr_{s}\big[V\rho V^{*}\big].

In order to understand the PPT and the entanglement breaking behavior of random (conjugate) unitary and orthogonal covariant channels, we need first to understand the large dd limit of the random variables λ1,2(d,s)\lambda_{1,2}^{(d,s)}. To start with, it follows from Lemma A.11 that the random variables λ1,2(d,s)\lambda_{1,2}^{(d,s)} have average and variance given by

𝔼⁡[λ1,2(d,s)]=1andVar⁡[λ1,2(d,s)]=s⁡(d2−1)(d​s)2−1.\mathbb{E}\Big[\lambda_{1,2}^{(d,s)}\Big]=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad\operatorname{Var}\Big[\lambda_{1,2}^{(d,s)}\Big]=\frac{s(d^{2}-1)}{(ds)^{2}-1}.

Note that although λ1,2(d,s)\lambda_{1,2}^{(d,s)} have the same first two moments, they do not have the same distribution, see Lemma A.11 for the exact moments of all orders. In fact, they have very different behavior as d→∞d\to\infty, as we shall see next. We first recall the definitions of the normal (or Gaussian) distribution of mean μ\mu and variance σ2\sigma^{2}:

X∼𝒩(m,σ2)⇔dX=12​π​σ2exp(−(x−m)22​σ2)dx,X\sim\mathcal{N}(m,\sigma^{2})\qquad\iff\qquad\mathrm{d}X=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}\exp\left(\frac{-(x-m)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)\mathrm{d}x,

and that of the Gamma distribution of parameters (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)

Y∼Γ(α,β)⇔dY=βαΓ⁡(α)yα−1exp⁡(−β​y)𝟏y>0dy.Y\sim\Gamma(\alpha,\beta)\qquad\iff\qquad\mathrm{d}Y=\frac{\beta^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}y^{\alpha-1}\exp(-\beta y)\mathbf{1}_{y>0}\mathrm{d}y.

Note that the Gamma distribution of parameters (1,λ)(1,\lambda) is also called the exponential distribution of parameter λ\lambda, for which we denote by 𝖤𝗑𝗉⁡(λ):=Γ⁡(1,λ)\mathsf{Exp}(\lambda):=\Gamma(1,\lambda).

Proposition 3.4.

As d→∞d\to\infty, the random variables λ1,2(d,s)\lambda_{1,2}^{(d,s)} behave as follows:

  1. (1)

    If ss is fixed, then

    • •

      the law of the random variable s​λ1(d,s)s\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)} converges in moments to the Gamma distribution Γ⁡(s,1)\Gamma(s,1)

    • •

      the law of the random variable s​λ2(d,s)s\lambda_{2}^{(d,s)} converges in moments to the normal distribution 𝒩⁡(s,s)\mathcal{N}(s,s).

  2. (2)

    If s=s⁡(d)→∞s=s(d)\to\infty, then

    λ1,2(d,s)→1​ in Lp for all p<∞.\lambda_{1,2}^{(d,s)}\to 1\text{ in $L^{p}$ for all $p<\infty$.}

    Furthermore, the same convergence holds almost surely if s≳dts\gtrsim d^{t} for some t>0t>0.

  3. (3)

    Moreover, for any t>0t>0, we have

    d−t​(λ1(d,s)−1)→0 and d−t​(λ2(d,s)−1)→0d^{-t}(\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}-1)\to 0\qquad\text{ and }\qquad d^{-t}(\lambda_{2}^{(d,s)}-1)\to 0

    almost surely as d→∞d\to\infty or s→∞s\to\infty (more precisely, this means that “d→∞d\to\infty and s=s⁡(d)s=s(d) arbitrary” or “s→∞s\to\infty and d=d⁡(s)d=d(s) arbitrary”).

Proof.

See Section A.2. ∎

We plot numerical realizations of the random variables λ1,2(d,s)\lambda_{1,2}^{(d,s)} against the theoretical curves in Figs. 4 and 5.

Theorem 3.5.

Let ΦU,U∼μd,sU,U\Phi_{U,U}\sim\mu^{U,U}_{d,s}, ΦU,U¯∼μd,sU,U¯\Phi_{U,\overline{U}}\sim\mu^{U,\overline{U}}_{d,s}, and ΦO,O∼μd,sO,O\Phi_{O,O}\sim\mu_{d,s}^{O,O} be, respectively, random (U,U)(U,U)-covariant, (U,U¯)(U,\overline{U})-covariant, and (O,O)(O,O)-covariant quantum channels.

  1. (1)

    Almost surely, as d→∞d\to\infty, ΦU,U\Phi_{U,U} is PPT and EB.

  2. (2)

    If ss is fixed, then

    limd→∞ℙ⁡(ΦU,U¯​ is PPT ⇔ EB)=limd→∞ℙ⁡(ΦO,O​ is PPT ⇔ EB)=ℙ⁡(Z≥−s)<1,\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi_{U,\overline{U}}\text{ is PPT $\Leftrightarrow$ EB})=\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi_{O,O}\text{ is PPT $\Leftrightarrow$ EB})=\mathbb{P}(Z\geq-\sqrt{s})<1,

    where Z∼𝒩⁡(0,1)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) is a standard normal random variable.

  3. (3)

    If s=s⁡(d)→∞s=s(d)\to\infty as d→∞d\to\infty, then

    limd→∞ℙ⁡(ΦU,U¯​ is PPT ⇔ EB)=limd→∞ℙ⁡(ΦO,O​ is PPT ⇔ EB)=1,\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi_{U,\overline{U}}\text{ is PPT $\Leftrightarrow$ EB})=\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi_{O,O}\text{ is PPT $\Leftrightarrow$ EB})=1,

    Furthermore, if s≳dts\gtrsim d^{t} for some t>0t>0, then almost surely as d→∞d\to\infty, ΦU,U¯\Phi_{U,\overline{U}} and ΦO,O\Phi_{O,O} are PPT and EB.

We remark that by the statement ‘Φ=Φd\Phi=\Phi_{d} is almost surely PPT/EB as d→∞d\to\infty’, we mean the eventual property of Φd\Phi_{d}: there exists an event set Ω\Omega of probability 1 such that for every ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega, there exists a number N=N⁡(ω)≥1N=N(\omega)\geq 1 such that Φd​(ω)\Phi_{d}(\omega) is PPT/EB for all d≥Nd\geq N. In particular, this implies that ℙ⁡(Φ​ is PPT/EB)→1\mathbb{P}(\Phi\text{ is PPT/EB})\to 1 as d→∞d\to\infty.

Proof.

We start with the first item, related to the unitary covariant channel ΦU,U\Phi_{U,U} and the random variable λ1(d,s)≥0\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}\geq 0. It follows from Proposition 3.4, (3) with t=1t=1, that, almost surely,

limd→∞λ1(d,s)d=0,\lim_{d\to\infty}\frac{\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}}{d}=0,

which yields (1) by Proposition 3.3.

Let us now move to the second point, corresponding to the regime ss fixed and the channels ΦU,U¯\Phi_{U,\overline{U}} and ΦO,O\Phi_{O,O}. From the previous point, we have that, almost surely as d→∞d\to\infty, λ1(d,s)≤d\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}\leq d; similarly for λ2(d,s)\lambda_{2}^{(d,s)}. The only constraint in Proposition 3.3 that we need to ensure is λ2(d,s)≥0\lambda_{2}^{(d,s)}\geq 0, and the conclusion follows from Proposition 3.4 (1): if Z~∼𝒩⁡(s,s)\tilde{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}(s,s), then

ℙ⁡(Z~≥0)=ℙ⁡(s​Z+s≥0)=ℙ⁡(Z≥−s),\mathbb{P}(\tilde{Z}\geq 0)=\mathbb{P}(\sqrt{s}Z+s\geq 0)=\mathbb{P}(Z\geq-\sqrt{s}),

for a standard normal random variable Z∼𝒩⁡(0,1)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).

Finally, regarding the proof of (3), the only constraint again is whether λ2(d,s)≥0\lambda_{2}^{(d,s)}\geq 0. Then the assertions follow directly from Proposition 3.4 (2): for the general regime s⁡(d)→∞s(d)\to\infty, λ2(d,s)→1\lambda_{2}^{(d,s)}\to 1 in probability, so we have

limd→∞ℙ⁡(ΦO,O​ is PPT)=limd→∞ℙ⁡(λ2(d,s)≥0)=1,\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi_{O,O}\text{ is PPT})=\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\lambda_{2}^{(d,s)}\geq 0)=1,

and analogously limd→∞ℙ⁡(ΦU,U¯​ is PPT)=1\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi_{U,\overline{U}}\text{ is PPT})=1. Furthermore, when s≳dts\gtrsim d^{t} for some t>0t>0, we have λ1,2(d,s)→1\lambda_{1,2}^{(d,s)}\to 1 hence 0≤λ1,2(d,s)≤d0\leq\lambda_{1,2}^{(d,s)}\leq d almost surely. ∎

Remark 3.6.

One can also show, by slightly modifying the previous arguments, that if s→∞s\to\infty, then, independently of the behavior of d=d⁡(s)d=d(s), all the three random channels ΦU,U\Phi_{U,U}, ΦU,U¯\Phi_{U,\overline{U}}, and ΦO,O\Phi_{O,O} are almost surely PPT and entanglement breaking.

In conclusion, we have shown that the equivalent PPT and EB properties for large (d→∞d\to\infty) random (conjugate) unitary and orthogonal covariant quantum channels are as follows:

  • •

    random unitary covariant channels are asymptotically PPT and EB (for any ss)

  • •

    random conjugate unitary and orthogonal covariant channels admit a phase transition between the regimes ss fixed and s→∞s\to\infty.

4. Random hyperoctahedral covariant channels

Here we consider a random behavior of the channels which are covariant with respect to hyperoctahedral group. Recall that one can realize the hyperoctahedral group of degree dd as the subgroup ℋd\mathcal{H}_{d} of the orthogonal group 𝒪d\mathcal{O}_{d} which is generated by diagonal orthogonal matrices and permutation matrices. The group ℋd\mathcal{H}_{d} is also known as the group of signed permutations and it has order 2d⋅d!2^{d}\cdot d!. It is recently shown [PJPY23, Proposition 4.4] that a linear map Φ:ℳd​(ℂ)→ℳd​(ℂ)\Phi:\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) is covariant with respect to the fundamental representation πℋd:H∈ℋd↦H∈𝒪d\pi_{\mathcal{H}_{d}}:H\in\mathcal{H}_{d}\mapsto H\in\mathcal{O}_{d} if and only if

(12) Φ⁡(Z)=p​Tr⁡(Z)d​Id+q​Z+r​Z⊤+s​diag​(Z),Z∈ℳd​(ℂ),\Phi(Z)=p\frac{\rm Tr(Z)}{d}I_{d}+qZ+rZ^{\top}+s\,{\rm diag}(Z),\;\;Z\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}),

for some p,q,r,s∈ℂp,q,r,s\in\mathbb{C}. In other words, the vector space of hyperoctahedral covariant linear maps is spanned by three quantum channels (the completely depolarizing, the identity, and the diagonal conditional expectation) and the transposition map. Note that the formula above covers the (conjugate) unitary and orthogonal covariant quantum channels discussed in Section 3.

Let us simply denote Cov⁡(H,H):=Cov⁡(πℋd,πℋd){\rm Cov}(H,H):={\rm Cov}(\pi_{\mathcal{H}_{d}},\pi_{\mathcal{H}_{d}}) and Inv⁡(H,H):=Inv⁡(πℋd⊗πℋd)=J⁡(Cov⁡(H,H)){\rm Inv}(H,H):={\rm Inv}(\pi_{\mathcal{H}_{d}}\otimes\pi_{\mathcal{H}_{d}})=J({\rm Cov}(H,H)) (by Proposition 2.4). Note that the Choi matrix of the map Φ\Phi given in (12) is

(13) J⁡(Φ)=p​Id2d+d​q​|Ωd⟩​⟨Ωd|+r​Fd+s​Πdiag∈Inv⁡(H⊗H),J(\Phi)=p\frac{I_{d^{2}}}{d}+dq|\Omega_{d}\rangle\langle\Omega_{d}|+rF_{d}+s\Pi_{\rm diag}\in{\rm Inv}(H\otimes H),

where |Ωd⟩=1d​∑i|i​i⟩|\Omega_{d}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\sum_{i}|ii\rangle and FdF_{d} are defined in Eqs. 6 and 7, and

Πdiag:=∑i=1d|i​i⟩​⟨i​i|\Pi_{\mathrm{diag}}:=\sum_{i=1}^{d}|ii\rangle\langle ii|

is the Choi matrix of the “diagonalization” (or completely dephasing) map Z↦diag⁡(Z)Z\mapsto\mathrm{diag}(Z). From this we can check that the space Inv⁡(H,H)=J⁡(Cov⁡(H,H)){\rm Inv}(H,H)=J({\rm Cov}(H,H)) is spanned by four mutually orthogonal projections

Π0\displaystyle\Pi_{0} =|Ωd⟩​⟨Ωd|,\displaystyle=|\Omega_{d}\rangle\langle\Omega_{d}|,
Π1\displaystyle\Pi_{1} =Πsym−Πdiag=Id2+F2−Πdiag,\displaystyle=\Pi_{\rm sym}-\Pi_{\rm diag}=\frac{I_{d^{2}}+F}{2}-\Pi_{\rm diag},
Π2\displaystyle\Pi_{2} =Πanti=Id2−F2,\displaystyle=\Pi_{\rm anti}=\frac{I_{d^{2}}-F}{2},
Π3\displaystyle\Pi_{3} =Πdiag−|Ωd⟩​⟨Ωd|.\displaystyle=\Pi_{\rm diag}-|\Omega_{d}\rangle\langle\Omega_{d}|.

Therefore, Proposition 2.2 gives the exact formula of 𝒯H⊗H:=𝒯πℋd⊗πℋd\mathcal{T}_{H\otimes H}:=\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{\mathcal{H}_{d}}\otimes\pi_{\mathcal{H}_{d}}},

(14) 𝒯H⊗H​X=∑i=03Tr⁡(Πi​X)​Πidi,X∈ℳd​(ℂ)⊗ℳd​(ℂ),\mathcal{T}_{H\otimes H}X=\sum_{i=0}^{3}{\Tr}(\Pi_{i}X)\frac{\Pi_{i}}{d_{i}},\;\;X\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}),

where the dimensions read d0=1d_{0}=1, d1=d2=d2−d2d_{1}=d_{2}=\frac{d^{2}-d}{2}, and d3=d−1d_{3}=d-1. We can now give the formula for the (H,H)(H,H)-twirling of a quantum channel.

Proposition 4.1.

Let Φ:ℳd​(ℂ)→ℳd​(ℂ)\Phi:\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) be a quantum channel. Then, the (H,H)(H,H) twirling of Φ\Phi is given by:

𝒯H,H(Φ)=p⋅Δ+q⋅id+r⋅⊤+(1−p−q−r)⋅diag\mathcal{T}_{H,H}(\Phi)=p\cdot\Delta+q\cdot\mathrm{id}+r\cdot\top+(1-p-q-r)\cdot\mathrm{diag}

where id,⊤,diag,Δ\mathrm{id},\top,\operatorname{diag},\Delta are, respectively, the identity, the transposition, the diagonalization, and the completely depolarizing linear maps. Here the coefficients p,q,rp,q,r are explicitly related to Φ\Phi by

p\displaystyle p =d−λ3​(Φ)d−1\displaystyle=\frac{d-\lambda_{3}(\Phi)}{d-1}
q\displaystyle q =λ1​(Φ)−λ3​(Φ)d2−d\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda_{1}(\Phi)-\lambda_{3}(\Phi)}{d^{2}-d}
r\displaystyle r =λ2​(Φ)−λ3​(Φ)d2−d,\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda_{2}(\Phi)-\lambda_{3}(\Phi)}{d^{2}-d},

where the parameters λ1,2,3​(Φ)\lambda_{1,2,3}(\Phi) associated to the channel are defined by (see also Figs. 2 and 6):

λ1​(Φ)\displaystyle\lambda_{1}(\Phi) =d⁡⟨Ωd|J⁡(Φ)|Ωd⟩\displaystyle=d\langle\Omega_{d}|J(\Phi)|\Omega_{d}\rangle
λ2​(Φ)\displaystyle\lambda_{2}(\Phi) =Tr⁡(J⁡(Φ)​Fd)\displaystyle=\Tr(J(\Phi)F_d)
λ3​(Φ)\displaystyle\lambda_{3}(\Phi) :=Tr⁡(J⁡(Φ)​Πdiag).\displaystyle:=\Tr(J(\Phi)\Pi_{\diag}).
Proof.

By Proposition 2.4 and Equation (14), we have

J⁡(𝒯H,H​Φ)\displaystyle J(\mathcal{T}_{H,H}\Phi) =𝒯H⊗H​(J⁡(Φ))=∑i=03Tr⁡(Πi​J​(Φ))​Πidi\displaystyle=\mathcal{T}_{H\otimes H}(J(\Phi))=\sum_{i=0}^{3}\Tr(\Pi_i J(\Phi))\frac{\Pi_{i}}{d_{i}}
=λ1d​|Ωd⟩​⟨Ωd|+(d+λ22−λ3)​Id2+Fd−2​Πdiagd2−d\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda_{1}}{d}|\Omega_{d}\rangle\langle\Omega_{d}|+\left(\frac{d+\lambda_{2}}{2}-\lambda_{3}\right)\frac{I_{d^{2}}+F_{d}-2\Pi_{\mathrm{diag}}}{d^{2}-d}
+d−λ22​Id2−Fdd2−d+(λ3−λ1d)​Πdiag−|Ωd⟩​⟨Ωd|d−1\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad+\frac{d-\lambda_{2}}{2}\frac{I_{d^{2}}-F_{d}}{d^{2}-d}+\left(\lambda_{3}-\frac{\lambda_{1}}{d}\right)\frac{\Pi_{\mathrm{diag}}-|\Omega_{d}\rangle\langle\Omega_{d}|}{d-1}
=d−λ3d−1​Id2d+λ1−λ3d2−d​d​|Ωd⟩​⟨Ωd|+λ2−λ3d2−d​Fd+(d+2)​λ3−λ1−λ2−dd2−d​Πdiag.\displaystyle=\frac{d-\lambda_{3}}{d-1}\frac{I_{d^{2}}}{d}+\frac{\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{3}}{d^{2}-d}d|\Omega_{d}\rangle\langle\Omega_{d}|+\frac{\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{3}}{d^{2}-d}F_{d}+\frac{(d+2)\lambda_{3}-\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}-d}{d^{2}-d}\Pi_{\mathrm{diag}}.

Here we used the fact Tr⁡(J⁡(Φ))=d\Tr(J(\Phi))=d since Φ\Phi is TP. ∎

One can now state the precise conditions for a (H,H)(H,H)-twirling of a quantum channel to be PPT; the PPT property has been shown in [PJPY23, Theorem 4.1] to be equivalent to the entanglement breaking property for hyperoctahedral covariant channels.

Proposition 4.2.

Given a quantum channel Φ:ℳd​(ℂ)→ℳd​(ℂ)\Phi:\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}), its (H,H)(H,H)-twirling 𝒯H,H​(Φ)\mathcal{T}_{H,H}(\Phi) is PPT iff it is EB iff

0\displaystyle 0 ≤λ3​(Φ)≤d,\displaystyle\leq\lambda_{3}(\Phi)\leq d,
(15) 0\displaystyle 0 ≤λ1​(Φ),λ2​(Φ)≤d​λ3​(Φ),\displaystyle\leq\lambda_{1}(\Phi),\lambda_{2}(\Phi)\leq d\lambda_{3}(\Phi),
2​λ3​(Φ)−d\displaystyle 2\lambda_{3}(\Phi)-d ≤λ1​(Φ),λ2​(Φ)≤d.\displaystyle\leq\lambda_{1}(\Phi),\lambda_{2}(\Phi)\leq d.
Proof.

The conditions in the statement are simply the following inequalities from [PJPY23, Eq. (4.17)] reformulated in terms of the parameters λ1,2,3​(Φ)\lambda_{1,2,3}(\Phi):

0\displaystyle 0 ≤p≤dd−1,\displaystyle\leq\,\,\,p\,\,\,\leq\frac{d}{d-1},
pd−1d−1\displaystyle\frac{p}{d}-\frac{1}{d-1} ≤q,r≤1−d−1d​p,\displaystyle\leq q,r\leq 1-\frac{d-1}{d}p,
−pd\displaystyle-\frac{p}{d} ≤q,r≤pd.\displaystyle\leq q,r\leq\frac{p}{d}.

∎

Now we consider a random Stinespring channel Φ:ℳd​(ℂ)→ℳd​(ℂ)\Phi:\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) with environment dimension ss and define the random hyperoctahedral covariant channel

ΦH,H:=𝒯H,H​(Φ)∼μd,sH,H.\Phi_{H,H}:=\mathcal{T}_{H,H}(\Phi)\sim\mu^{H,H}_{d,s}.

Since the PPT (and therefore the EB) property of the twirled channel 𝒯H,H​(Φ)\mathcal{T}_{H,H}(\Phi) depends only on the three parameters λ1,2,3​(Φ)\lambda_{1,2,3}(\Phi), we shall consider the corresponding random variables associated to the random channel:

λ1(d,s)=d⁡⟨Ωd|J⁡(Φ)|Ωd⟩,λ2(d,s)=Tr⁡(J⁡(Φ)​Fd),λ3(d,s):=Tr⁡(J⁡(Φ)​Πdiag).\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}=d\langle\Omega_{d}|J(\Phi)|\Omega_{d}\rangle,\quad\lambda_{2}^{(d,s)}=\Tr(J(\Phi)F_d),\quad\lambda_{3}^{(d,s)}:=\Tr(J(\Phi)\Pi_{\diag}).

The asymptotic behavior of the first two variables has been studied in the previous section, Proposition 3.4; we now turn to the study of λ3(d,s)\lambda_{3}^{(d,s)}. The average and the variance of this random variable are given by (Lemma A.11)

𝔼⁡[λ3(d,s)]=1andVar⁡[λ3(d,s)]=1d​s+1.\mathbb{E}\Big[\lambda_{3}^{(d,s)}\Big]=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad\operatorname{Var}\Big[\lambda_{3}^{(d,s)}\Big]=\frac{1}{ds+1}.
Proposition 4.3.

The following almost sure convergence holds, independently of the scaling of the parameter ss:

limd→∞λ3(d,s)=1.\lim_{d\to\infty}\lambda_{3}^{(d,s)}=1.
Proof.

See Section A.2. ∎

We can now prove the main result of this section, giving the PPT and EB properties of a hyperoctahedral covariant random channel, in the d→∞d\to\infty regime.

Theorem 4.4.

Let ΦH,H∼μd,sH,H\Phi_{H,H}\sim\mu^{H,H}_{d,s} be a random (H,H)(H,H)-covariant quantum channel. Then:

  1. (1)

    If ss is fixed,

    limd→∞ℙ⁡(ΦH,H​ is PPT ⇔ EB)=ℙ⁡(Z≥−s)<1,\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi_{H,H}\text{ is PPT $\Leftrightarrow$ EB})=\mathbb{P}(Z\geq-\sqrt{s})<1,

    where Z∼𝒩⁡(0,1)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) is a standard normal random variable.

  2. (2)

    If s=s⁡(d)→∞s=s(d)\to\infty as d→∞d\to\infty, then

    limd→∞ℙ⁡(ΦH,H​ is PPT ⇔ EB)=1.\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi_{H,H}\text{ is PPT $\Leftrightarrow$ EB})=1.

    Furthermore, if s≳dts\gtrsim d^{t} for some t>0t>0, then almost surely as d→∞d\to\infty, ΦH,H\Phi_{H,H} is PPT and EB.

Proof.

Since λ3(d,s)→1\lambda_{3}^{(d,s)}\to 1 as d→∞d\to\infty, the equations (15) reduce to the conditions from Proposition 3.3 (3). The proof is now the same as Theorem 3.5 (2) and (3). ∎

Note that

𝒯U,U¯∘𝒯H,H=𝒯U,U¯,𝒯U,U∘𝒯H,H=𝒯U,U,and𝒯O,O∘𝒯H,H=𝒯O,O,\mathcal{T}_{U,\overline{U}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{H,H}=\mathcal{T}_{U,\overline{U}},\quad\mathcal{T}_{U,U}\circ\mathcal{T}_{H,H}=\mathcal{T}_{U,U},\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{T}_{O,O}\circ\mathcal{T}_{H,H}=\mathcal{T}_{O,O},

by Proposition 2.3 and Proposition 2.4. Since the twirling operations preserve both PPT and entanglement breaking properties, Theorem 4.4 directly implies the asymptotic PPT and EB behavior of random depolarizing / transpose depolarizing / orthogonal covariant channels, in the regime where s≳dts\gtrsim d^{t} with d→∞d\to\infty, recovering part of Theorem 3.5.

Corollary 4.5.

Suppose s≳dts\gtrsim d^{t} for some constants t>0t>0. Then almost surely, the random depolarizing channel 𝒯U,U¯​Φ\mathcal{T}_{U,\overline{U}}\Phi, the random transpose depolarizing channel 𝒯U,U​Φ\mathcal{T}_{U,U}\Phi, and the random orthogonal covariant channel 𝒯O,O​Φ\mathcal{T}_{O,O}\Phi are PPT and EB, as d→∞d\to\infty.

In conclusion, we have shown that the equivalent PPT and EB properties for large (d→∞d\to\infty) random hyperoctahedral covariant quantum channels admit a phase transition between the regimes ss fixed and s→∞s\to\infty, which is completely parallel with random conjugate unitary and orthogonal covariant channels.

5. Random diagonal orthogonal covariant channels

In this section, we consider random quantum channels which are covariant with respect to the actions of the diagonal unitary group

𝒟𝒰d:={diag(z):z∈ℂd,|zi|=1∀i∈[d]}\mathcal{DU}_{d}:=\big\{\mathrm{diag}(z)\,:\,z\in\mathbb{C}^{d},\,|z_{i}|=1\quad\forall i\in[d]\big\}

and the diagonal orthogonal group

𝒟​𝒪d:={diag⁡(ε):ε∈{±1}d}.\mathcal{DO}_{d}:=\big\{\mathrm{diag}(\varepsilon)\,:\,\varepsilon\in\{\pm 1\}^{d}\big\}.

Bipartite quantum states that are invariant with respect to the actions of the groups above, as well as channels that are covariant for these actions have appeared in the literature in the last 20 years [DSS+00, CK06, Liu15, LS15, SBSGS22], but have been studied in detail in [SN21]. Since, they have found many applications, see e.g. [SN22a, SN22b, SDN22]. We recall from [SN21, Definition 6.3] that a quantum channel Φ:ℳd​(ℂ)→ℳd​(ℂ)\Phi:\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) is called:

  • •

    conjugate diagonal unitary covariant (CDUC) if

    ∀Z∈ℳd​(ℂ)​ and ​U∈𝒟​𝒰d:Φ⁡(U​Z​U∗)=U∗​Φ​(Z)​U,\forall Z\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\text{ and }U\in\mathcal{DU}_{d}:\qquad\Phi(UZU^{*})=U^{*}\Phi(Z)U,
  • •

    diagonal unitary covariant (DUC) if

    ∀Z∈ℳd​(ℂ)​ and ​U∈𝒟​𝒰d:Φ⁡(U​Z​U∗)=U​Φ​(Z)​U∗,\forall Z\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\text{ and }U\in\mathcal{DU}_{d}:\qquad\Phi(UZU^{*})=U\Phi(Z)U^{*},
  • •

    diagonal orthogonal covariant (DOC) if

    ∀Z∈ℳd​(ℂ)​ and ​O∈𝒟​𝒪d:Φ⁡(O​Z​O)=O​Φ​(Z)​O.\forall Z\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\text{ and }O\in\mathcal{DO}_{d}:\qquad\Phi(OZO)=O\Phi(Z)O.

Note that we employ a different naming convention than the one in [SN21], by interchanging the DUC and CDUC terms. In the present work, the emphasis is on the covariance property, hence we prefer to use the “conjugate” adjective for the case where πB=πA¯\pi_{B}=\overline{\pi_{A}}.

The structure of linear maps satisfying the covariance conditions above has been obtained in [SN21, Eqs. (36)-(38)]: a linear map Φ:ℳd​(ℂ)→ℳd​(ℂ)\Phi:\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) is

  • •

    CDUC if there exists a pair A,C∈ℳd​(ℂ)A,C\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) such that diag​A=diag​C\mathrm{diag}A=\mathrm{diag}C and

    ∀Z∈ℳd​(ℂ)Φ⁡(Z)=ΦA,C(1)​(Z)=diag⁡(A​|diag⁡(Z)⟩)+C∘⊙Z⊤.\forall Z\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\qquad\Phi(Z)=\Phi^{(1)}_{A,C}(Z)=\mathrm{diag}(A\ket{\mathrm{diag}(Z)})+\accentset{\circ}{C}\odot Z^{\top}.
  • •

    DUC if there exists a pair A,B∈ℳd​(ℂ)A,B\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) such that diag​A=diag​B\mathrm{diag}A=\mathrm{diag}B and

    ∀Z∈ℳd​(ℂ)Φ⁡(Z)=ΦA,B(2)​(Z)=diag⁡(A​|diag⁡(Z)⟩)+B∘⊙Z.\forall Z\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\qquad\Phi(Z)=\Phi^{(2)}_{A,B}(Z)=\mathrm{diag}(A\ket{\mathrm{diag}(Z)})+\accentset{\circ}{B}\odot Z.
  • •

    DOC if there exists a triple A,B,C∈ℳd​(ℂ)A,B,C\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) such that diag​A=diag​B=diag​C\mathrm{diag}A=\mathrm{diag}B=\mathrm{diag}C and

    ∀Z∈ℳd​(ℂ)Φ⁡(Z)=ΦA,B,C(3)​(Z)=diag⁡(A​|diag⁡(Z)⟩)+B∘⊙Z+C∘⊙Z⊤.\forall Z\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\qquad\Phi(Z)=\Phi^{(3)}_{A,B,C}(Z)=\mathrm{diag}(A\ket{\mathrm{diag}(Z)})+\accentset{\circ}{B}\odot Z+\accentset{\circ}{C}\odot Z^{\top}.

Above, the notation X∘\accentset{\circ}{X}, for a matrix X∈ℳd​(ℂ)X\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}), denotes the matrix XX without its diagonal, i.e.

X∘:=X−diag​X or (X∘)i​j={Xi​j if ​i≠j0 if ​i=j.\accentset{\circ}{X}:=X-\mathrm{diag}X\qquad\text{ or }\qquad(\accentset{\circ}{X})_{ij}=\begin{cases}X_{ij}\qquad&\text{ if }i\neq j\\ 0\qquad&\text{ if }i=j.\end{cases}

Note that the maps Φ(1,2)\Phi^{(1,2)} can be seen as special cases of the DOC map Φ(3)\Phi^{(3)} by setting, respectively, B=diag​BB=\mathrm{diag}B and C=diag​CC=\mathrm{diag}C. A linear DOC map ΦA,B,C(3)\Phi^{(3)}_{A,B,C} is completely positive (CP) iff

  • •

    AA is entrywise nonnegative: Ai​j≥0A_{ij}\geq 0 for all i,j∈[d]i,j\in[d]

  • •

    BB is positive semidefinite: B≥0B\geq 0

  • •

    CC is selfadjoint and |Ci​j|2≤Ai​j​Aj​i|C_{ij}|^{2}\leq A_{ij}A_{ji} for all i,j∈[d]i,j\in[d].

A linear DOC map ΦA,B,C(3)\Phi^{(3)}_{A,B,C} is trace preserving (TP) iff AA is column stochastic, i.e.

∀j∈[d]∑i=1dAi​j=1.\forall j\in[d]\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{d}A_{ij}=1.

It is important to note at this point that the sets of CDUC, DUC, and DOC linear maps or quantum channels are parametrized by a pair or a triple of d×dd\times d matrices satisfying certain conditions; the number of parameters in these models is growing with the dimension dd. This fact is in stark contrast with the symmetries investigated in Section 3 (full-unitary and full-orthogonal) and in Section 4 (hyperoctahedral). It is the richness of these models that allows for the existence of PPT symmetric channels that are not entanglement breaking, as we show next. Let us first discuss the PPT property for diagonal symmetric channels.

Proposition 5.1 ([SN21]).

For any triple of matrices A,B,C∈ℳd​(ℂ)A,B,C\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) having the same diagonal, we have

Φ(1)A,C∘⊤=Φ(2)A,C,Φ(2)A,B∘⊤=Φ(1)A,B,Φ(3)A,B,C∘⊤=Φ(3)A,C,B.\Phi^{(1)}_{A,C}\circ\top=\Phi^{(2)}_{A,C},\qquad\Phi^{(2)}_{A,B}\circ\top=\Phi^{(1)}_{A,B},\qquad\Phi^{(3)}_{A,B,C}\circ\top=\Phi^{(3)}_{A,C,B}.

Hence, we have the following characterizations of the PPT property:

  • •

    A CDUC quantum channel ΦA,C(1)\Phi^{(1)}_{A,C} is PPT iff CC is positive semidefinite (C≥0C\geq 0).

  • •

    A DUC quantum channel ΦA,B(2)\Phi^{(2)}_{A,B} is PPT iff |Bi​j|2≤Ai​j​Aj​i|B_{ij}|^{2}\leq A_{ij}A_{ji} for all i,j∈[d]i,j\in[d].

  • •

    A DOC quantum channel ΦA,B,C(3)\Phi^{(3)}_{A,B,C} is PPT iff CC is positive semidefinite (C≥0C\geq 0) and |Bi​j|2≤Ai​j​Aj​i|B_{ij}|^{2}\leq A_{ij}A_{ji} for all i,j∈[d]i,j\in[d].

To characterize the entanglement breaking property. we recall the following two important definitions from [JM19] and [NS21]:

  • •

    A pair of matrices A,B∈ℳd​(ℂ)A,B\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) having the same diagonal is said to be pairwise completely positive (PCP) if there exist matrices V,W∈ℳd×k​(ℂ)V,W\in\mathcal{M}_{d\times k}(\mathbb{C}), for some k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, such that the following decomposition holds:

    A=(V⊙V¯)​(W⊙W¯)∗,B=(V⊙W)​(V⊙W)∗.A=(V\odot\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5muV\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu)(W\odot\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5muW\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu)^{*},\qquad B=(V\odot W)(V\odot W)^{*}.
  • •

    A triple of matrices A,B,C∈ℳd​(ℂ)A,B,C\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) having the same diagonal is said to be triplewise completely positive (TCP) if there exist matrices V,W∈ℳd×k​(ℂ)V,W\in\mathcal{M}_{d\times k}(\mathbb{C}), for some k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, such that the following decomposition holds:

    A=(V⊙V¯)​(W⊙W¯)∗,B=(V⊙W)​(V⊙W)∗,C=(V⊙W¯)​(V⊙W¯)∗.A=(V\odot\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5muV\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu)(W\odot\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5muW\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu)^{*},\qquad B=(V\odot W)(V\odot W)^{*},\qquad C=(V\odot\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5muW\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu)(V\odot\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5muW\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu)^{*}.
Proposition 5.2 ([SN21]).

For any triple of matrices A,B,C∈ℳd​(ℂ)A,B,C\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) having the same diagonal, we have

  • •

    A CDUC quantum channel ΦA,C(1)\Phi^{(1)}_{A,C} is EB iff the pair (A,C)(A,C) is pairwise completely positive (PCP).

  • •

    A DUC quantum channel ΦA,B(2)\Phi^{(2)}_{A,B} is EB iff the pair (A,B)(A,B) is pairwise completely positive (PCP).

  • •

    A DOC quantum channel ΦA,B,C(3)\Phi^{(3)}_{A,B,C} is EB iff the triple (A,B,C)(A,B,C) is triplewise completely positive (TCP).

Importantly, for the diagonal covariant channels discussed in this section, the EB property is not equivalent to the PPT property: there exist PPT channels that are not entanglement breaking. Such examples can be found in a simple way starting from the PPT entangled states of size 3×33\times 3 in [KKL11, KO12] or from nonnegative and positive semidefinite matrices of size d≥5d\geq 5 which are not completely positive [BSM03, TAQ+18, Yu16, SN21].

Let us now provide the formulas for the diagonal twirlings of a quantum channels. We would like to point out again that our naming convention here is different from the one in [SN21], in the sense that the terms DUC and CDUC are swapped.

Proposition 5.3 ([NS21, Section 6]).

Let Φ:ℳd​(ℂ)→ℳd​(ℂ)\Phi:\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) be a linear map. Then, its twirlings with respect to the diagonal groups 𝒟​𝒰d\mathcal{DU}_{d} and 𝒟​𝒪d\mathcal{DO}_{d} are given by

𝒯𝖢𝖣𝖴𝖢​Φ\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{CDUC}}\Phi :=𝒯𝒟​𝒰d,𝒟​𝒰¯d​Φ=ΦA⁡(Φ),C⁡(Φ)(1)\displaystyle:=\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{DU}_{d},\overline{\mathcal{DU}}_{d}}\Phi=\Phi^{(1)}_{A(\Phi),C(\Phi)}
𝒯𝖣𝖴𝖢​Φ\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{DUC}}\Phi :=𝒯𝒟​𝒰d,𝒟​𝒰d​Φ=ΦA⁡(Φ),B⁡(Φ)(2)\displaystyle:=\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{DU}_{d},\mathcal{DU}_{d}}\Phi=\Phi^{(2)}_{A(\Phi),B(\Phi)}
𝒯𝖣𝖮𝖢​Φ\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{DOC}}\Phi :=𝒯𝒟​𝒪d,𝒟​𝒪d​Φ=ΦA⁡(Φ),B⁡(Φ),C⁡(Φ)(3),\displaystyle:=\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{DO}_{d},\mathcal{DO}_{d}}\Phi=\Phi^{(3)}_{A(\Phi),B(\Phi),C(\Phi)},

where the matrices A,B,CA,B,C are defined by (See Fig. 7 for a graphical representation):

A(Φ)i​j=⟨ij|J(Φ)|ij⟩,B(Φ)i​j=⟨ii|J(Φ)|jj⟩,andC(Φ)i​j=⟨ij|J(Φ)|ji⟩∀i,j∈[d].A(\Phi)_{ij}=\langle ij|J(\Phi)|ij\rangle,\quad B(\Phi)_{ij}=\langle ii|J(\Phi)|jj\rangle,\quad\text{and}\quad C(\Phi)_{ij}=\langle ij|J(\Phi)|ji\rangle\qquad\forall i,j\in[d].

Let us now consider random diagonal covariant channels. To this end, let ΦV:ℳd​(ℂ)→ℳd​(ℂ)\Phi_{V}:\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) be a random Stinespring channel with environment dimension ss and define the following classes of random symmetric channels:

  • •

    random CDUC channels

    Φ𝖢𝖣𝖴𝖢:=𝒯𝖢𝖣𝖴𝖢​(ΦV)∼μd,s𝖢𝖣𝖴𝖢.\Phi_{\mathsf{CDUC}}:=\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{CDUC}}(\Phi_{V})\sim\mu^{\mathsf{CDUC}}_{d,s}.
  • •

    random DUC channels

    Φ𝖣𝖴𝖢:=𝒯𝖣𝖴𝖢​(ΦV)∼μd,s𝖣𝖴𝖢.\Phi_{\mathsf{DUC}}:=\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{DUC}}(\Phi_{V})\sim\mu^{\mathsf{DUC}}_{d,s}.
  • •

    random DOC channels

    Φ𝖣𝖮𝖢:=𝒯𝖣𝖮𝖢​(ΦV)∼μd,s𝖣𝖮𝖢.\Phi_{\mathsf{DOC}}:=\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{DOC}}(\Phi_{V})\sim\mu^{\mathsf{DOC}}_{d,s}.

Since the PPT and EB properties of the random channels we consider here are determined by the associated A,B,CA,B,C matrices, we shall study the corresponding random matrices, derived from the Haar-distributed random isometry V:ℂd→ℂd⊗ℂsV:\mathbb{C}^{d}\to\mathbb{C}^{d}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{s}:

(16) A=∑k=1sV(k)⊙V(k)¯,B=∑k=1s|diag​V(k)⟩​⟨diag​V(k)|,C=∑k=1sV(k)⊙(V(k))∗,A=\sum_{k=1}^{s}V^{(k)}\odot\overline{V^{(k)}},\quad B=\sum_{k=1}^{s}|{\rm diag\,}V^{(k)}\rangle\langle{\rm diag\,}V^{(k)}|,\quad C=\sum_{k=1}^{s}V^{(k)}\odot(V^{(k)})^{*},

where VV is represented in the block matrix form V=(V(1)V(s))V=\begin{pmatrix}V^{(1)}\\ \vdots\\ V^{(s)}\end{pmatrix} for V(k)∈ℳd​(ℂ)V^{(k)}\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}). Moreover, we can draw the diagrams of A,B,CA,B,C as in Fig. 8. Note that these A,B,C∈ℳd​(ℂ)A,B,C\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) and their distribution depends on the integer parameter s≥1s\geq 1.

Remark 5.4.

It is useful to connect the random parameters A,B,CA,B,C discussed in this section to the scalars λ1,2,3(d,s)\lambda_{1,2,3}^{(d,s)} from Sections 3 and 4; graphically, compare Figs. 3 and 6 with Fig. 8. We have the following relations:

λ1​(Φ)=∑i,j=1d⟨i|B⁡(Φ)|j⟩=Tr⁡(Jd​B​(Φ)),\displaystyle\lambda_{1}(\Phi)=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}\langle i|B(\Phi)|j\rangle=\Tr(J_d B(\Phi)),
λ2​(Φ)=∑i,j=1d⟨i|C⁡(Φ)|j⟩=Tr⁡(Jd​C​(Φ)),\displaystyle\lambda_{2}(\Phi)=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}\langle i|C(\Phi)|j\rangle=\Tr(J_d C(\Phi)),
(17) λ3​(Φ)=Tr⁡A⁡(Φ)=Tr⁡B⁡(Φ)=Tr⁡C⁡(Φ),\displaystyle\lambda_{3}(\Phi)=\Tr A(\Phi)=\Tr B(\Phi)=\Tr C(\Phi),

where Jd∈ℳd​(ℂ)J_{d}\in\mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbb{C}) is the matrix in which all entries are equal to 1.

As in the previous two sections, we study now the asymptotic behavior of three random matrix parameters A,B,CA,B,C in the regime d→∞d\to\infty. The following results will be used to establish, later in this section, the PPT and the EB properties of random CDUC, DUC, and DOC channels. Since both the entrywise and the spectral distributions of the matrices A,B,CA,B,C are needed (see e.g. Proposition 5.1), the analysis in this section is more involved. We defer the technical proofs of the following three results, Propositions 5.5, 5.8 and 5.9, to Section A.3.

We start by giving the large-dd limit spectrum of the self-adjoint matrix C∈ℳds​a​(ℂ)C\in\mathcal{M}^{sa}_{d}(\mathbb{C}), whose positive semi-definiteness is needed for PPT property of DOC channels. We recall that the semicircular distribution with average mm and variance σ2\sigma^{2} is given by

dSCm,σ=4​σ2−(x−m)22​π​σ​𝟏[−2​σ+m,2​σ+m]​(x)​d​x.\mathrm{d}\mathrm{SC}_{m,\sigma}=\frac{\sqrt{4\sigma^{2}-(x-m)^{2}}}{2\pi\sigma}\mathbf{1}_{[-2\sigma+m,2\sigma+m]}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x.
Proposition 5.5.

The asymptotic spectral behavior of the random matrix CC, as d→∞d\to\infty, is given as follows:

  1. (1)

    In the regime s/d→0s/d\to 0,

    • •

      in probability, the empirical spectral distribution of (d​s)1/2​C(ds)^{1/2}C converges, in moment, to a semicircular distribution with mean 00 and variance 1,

    • •

      almost surely, we have the following convergence of the first three moments of (d​s)1/2​C(ds)^{1/2}C:

      1d​Tr⁡((d​s)1/2​C)→0,1d​Tr⁡(d​s​C2)→1,1d​Tr⁡((d​s)3/2​C3)→0.\frac{1}{d}\Tr((ds)^{1/2}C)\to 0,\quad\frac{1}{d}\Tr(ds C^2)\to 1,\quad\frac{1}{d}\Tr((ds)^{3/2}C^3)\to 0.
  2. (2)

    In the regime s∼c​ds\sim cd for a constant c>0c>0, the empirical spectral distribution of s​CsC converges, in moments, to a semicircular distribution with mean cc and variance cc almost surely.

  3. (3)

    In the regime s/d→∞s/d\to\infty, the empirical spectral distribution of d​CdC converges, in moments, to the probability mass δ1\delta_{1} almost surely.

Proof.

See Section A.3. ∎

Under some slightly stronger hypothesis, the convergence in moments in item (3) above can be upgraded to a convergence in operator norm.

Proposition 5.6.

When s≳d1+ts\gtrsim d^{1+t} for some constant t>0t>0, ‖d​C−Id‖∞→0\|dC-I_{d}\|_{\infty}\to 0 almost surely as d→∞d\to\infty. In particular, the minimum eigenvalue λmin​(d​C)\lambda_{\min}(dC) of d​CdC converges to 1 almost surely as d→∞d\to\infty.

Proof.

See Section A.3. ∎

Remark 5.7.

Although it is not needed in our work, we can show the convergence of matrix BB in various regimes, using the same method. For example, in the regime s∼c​ds\sim cd and d→∞d\to\infty, the the empirical spectral distribution of s​BsB converges, almost surely, to a Marc̆enko-Pastur distribution of parameter cc: the distribution MPc{\rm MP}_{c} given by

dMPc=max⁡(1−c,0)​δ0+(b−x)​(x−a)2​π​x​ 1[a,b]​(x)​d​x,\mathrm{d}\mathrm{MP}_{c}=\max(1-c,0)\delta_{0}+\frac{\sqrt{(b-x)(x-a)}}{2\pi x}\;\mathbf{1}_{[a,b]}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,

with a=(1−c)2a=(1-\sqrt{c})^{2} and b=(1+c)2b=(1+\sqrt{c})^{2}.

We now turn to the distribution of the elements of the matrices A,B,CA,B,C.

Proposition 5.8.

When ss is fixed, we have as d→∞d\to\infty,

  1. (1)

    the law of d​s​Ai​jdsA_{ij} converges, in moments, to the Gamma distribution Γ⁡(s,1)\Gamma(s,1),

  2. (2)

    both the laws of |d​s​Bi​j|2|dsB_{ij}|^{2} and |d​s​Ci​j|2|dsC_{ij}|^{2} converge, in moments, to that of the product of two independent random variables X∼Γ⁡(s,1)X\sim\Gamma(s,1) and Y∼𝖤𝗑𝗉⁡(1)Y\sim\mathsf{Exp}(1),

    for any fixed N≤d/2N\leq d/2 and pairwise distinct indices i1,…,iN,j1,…,jN∈[d]i_{1},\ldots,i_{N},j_{1},\ldots,j_{N}\in[d], the 3​N3N random variables

    d​s​Ai1​j1,d​s​Aj1​i1,|d​s​Bi1​j1|2,d​s​Ai2​j2,d​s​Aj2​i2,|d​s​Bi2​j2|2,…,d​s​AiN​jN,d​s​AjN​iN,|d​s​BiN​jN|2dsA_{i_{1}j_{1}},dsA_{j_{1}i_{1}},|dsB_{i_{1}j_{1}}|^{2},dsA_{i_{2}j_{2}},dsA_{j_{2}i_{2}},|dsB_{i_{2}j_{2}}|^{2},\ldots,dsA_{i_{N}j_{N}},dsA_{j_{N}i_{N}},|dsB_{i_{N}j_{N}}|^{2}

    are asymptotically independent.

See Section A.3. ∎

Proposition 5.9.

When s≳dts\gtrsim d^{t} for some constant t>0t>0, we have the following almost sure convergences as d→∞d\to\infty:

    maxi,j⁡|d​Ai​j−1|→0\displaystyle\max_{i,j}|dA_{ij}-1|\to 0 (in particular, maxi,j⁡d​Ai​j→1\displaystyle\max_{i,j}dA_{ij}\to 1 and mini,j⁡d​Ai​j→1\displaystyle\min_{i,j}dA_{ij}\to 1).

    maxi≠j⁡d1+t′/2​|Bi​j|→0\displaystyle\max_{i\neq j}d^{1+t^{\prime}/2}|B_{ij}|\to 0 whenever t′<tt^{\prime}<t.

    maxi≠j⁡d1+t′/2​|Ci​j|→0\displaystyle\max_{i\neq j}d^{1+t^{\prime}/2}|C_{ij}|\to 0 whenever t′<tt^{\prime}<t.

See Section A.3. ∎

The previous three results allow us to establish the PPT property for diagonal unitary and orthogonal covariant random channels. Note the qualitatively different behaviors for the DUC case versus the CDUC and DOC symmetries.

Theorem 5.10.

Let Φ𝖣𝖴𝖢∼μd,s𝖣𝖴𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{DUC}}\sim\mu^{\mathsf{DUC}}_{d,s} be a random DUC channel. Then:

  1. (1)

    In the regime ss is fixed and d→∞d\to\infty, we have

    limd→∞ℙ⁡(Φ𝖣𝖴𝖢​ is PPT )=0.\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi_{\mathsf{DUC}}\text{ is PPT })=0.
  2. (2)

    In the regime s≳dts\gtrsim d^{t} for some constant t>0t>0, Φ𝖣𝖴𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{DUC}} is almost surely PPT as d→∞d\to\infty.

Let Φ𝖢𝖣𝖴𝖢∼μd,s𝖢𝖣𝖴𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{CDUC}}\sim\mu^{\mathsf{CDUC}}_{d,s}, and Φ𝖣𝖮𝖢∼μd,s𝖣𝖮𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{DOC}}\sim\mu^{\mathsf{DOC}}_{d,s} be, respectively, random CDUC and DOC channels. Then:

  1. (3)

    In the regime d→∞d\to\infty and s/d→0s/d\to 0, almost surely, neither Φ𝖢𝖣𝖴𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{CDUC}} nor Φ𝖣𝖮𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{DOC}} are PPT.

  2. (4)

    Consider the regime s∼c​ds\sim cd. If c<4c<4, then almost surely as d→∞d\to\infty, neither Φ𝖢𝖣𝖴𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{CDUC}} nor Φ𝖣𝖮𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{DOC}} are PPT. If c>4c>4, then almost surely as d→∞d\to\infty, both Φ𝖢𝖣𝖴𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{CDUC}} and Φ𝖣𝖮𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{DOC}} have Choi matrices whose partial transpositions converge, in moments, to a probability measure supported on the positive real line.

  3. (5)

    In the regime s≳d1+ts\gtrsim d^{1+t} for some constant t>0t>0, both Φ𝖢𝖣𝖴𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{CDUC}} and Φ𝖣𝖮𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{DOC}} are almost surely PPT as d→∞d\to\infty.

Proof.

Let us start with the first and second points. By Proposition 5.1, we know that

Φ𝖣𝖴𝖢​ is PPT ⇔Ai​j​Aj​i≥|Bi​j|2​∀i≠j.\Phi_{\mathsf{DUC}}\text{ is PPT }\iff A_{ij}A_{ji}\geq|B_{ij}|^{2}\;\;\forall\,i\neq j.

If ss is fixed, then by Proposition 5.8, the limit probability can be estimated, for any fixed N≥1N\geq 1, as follows:

lim supd→∞ℙ⁡(Φ𝖣𝖴𝖢​ is PPT )\displaystyle\limsup_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi_{\mathsf{DUC}}\text{ is PPT }) ≤lim supd→∞ℙ(A2​n−1,2​nA2​n,2​n−1≥|B2​n−1,2​n|2∀n=1,…,N)\displaystyle\leq\limsup_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(A_{2n-1,2n}A_{2n,2n-1}\geq|B_{2n-1,2n}|^{2}\;\forall\,n=1,\ldots,N)
=∏n=1Nlimd→∞ℙ⁡((d​s​A2​n−1,2​n)⋅(d​s​A2​n,2​n−1)≥|d​s​B2​n−1,2​n|2)\displaystyle=\prod_{n=1}^{N}\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}((dsA_{2n-1,2n})\cdot(dsA_{2n,2n-1})\geq|dsB_{2n-1,2n}|^{2})
=(ℙ⁡(X1​X2≥X3​Y))N,\displaystyle=\left(\mathbb{P}(X_{1}X_{2}\geq X_{3}Y)\right)^{N},

where X1,X2,X3,YX_{1},X_{2},X_{3},Y are four independent random variables such that X1,X2,X3∼Γ⁡(s,1)X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}\sim\Gamma(s,1) and Y∼𝖤𝗑𝗉⁡(1)Y\sim\mathsf{Exp}(1). Moreover, the last equation can be more explicitly written as an integral

ℙ⁡(X1​X2≥X3​Y)=∫ℝ4𝟏{x1​x2≥x3​y,x1,x2,x3,y≥0}​(x1​x2​x3)s−1((s−1)!)3​e−(x1+x2+x3+y)​d​x1​d​x2​d​x3​𝑑y<1.\mathbb{P}(X_{1}X_{2}\geq X_{3}Y)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4}}\mathbf{1}_{\big\{\begin{subarray}{c}x_{1}x_{2}\geq x_{3}y,\\ x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},y\geq 0\end{subarray}\big\}}\frac{(x_{1}x_{2}x_{3})^{s-1}}{((s-1)!)^{3}}e^{-(x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}+y)}dx_{1}\,dx_{2}\,dx_{3}\,dy<1.

Therefore, we have (1) by taking N→∞N\to\infty. When s≳dts\gtrsim d^{t} for some t>0t>0, we can show that d2​mini≠j⁡(Ai​j​Aj​i−|Bi​j|2)→1d^{2}\min_{i\neq j}(A_{ij}A_{ji}-|B_{ij}|^{2})\to 1, almost surely, from the inequality

(mini,j⁡d​Ai​j)2−(maxi≠j⁡d​|Bi​j|)2≤d2​mini≠j⁡(Ai​j​Aj​i−|Bi​j|2)≤(maxi,j⁡d​Ai​j)2\left(\min_{i,j}dA_{ij}\right)^{2}-\left(\max_{i\neq j}d|B_{ij}|\right)^{2}\leq d^{2}\min_{i\neq j}(A_{ij}A_{ji}-|B_{ij}|^{2})\leq\left(\max_{i,j}dA_{ij}\right)^{2}

and Proposition 5.9, and hence (2) is shown.

Now let us focus on (3) - (5), namely the PPT behaviors of CDUC and DOC channels. Note that for both two channels, their PPT property requires the condition C≥0C\geq 0, and in particular, this implies that

Tr⁡C​Tr⁡C3≥(Tr⁡C2)2\Tr C\Tr C^{3}\geq(\Tr C^{2})^{2}

by Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. However, when s/d→0s/d\to 0 as d→∞d\to\infty, we have by Proposition 5.5 (1)

s2​(Tr⁡C​Tr⁡C3−(Tr⁡C2)2)=1d​Tr⁡((d​s)1/2​C)⋅1d​Tr⁡((d​s)3/2​C3)−(1d​Tr⁡(d​s​C2))2→−1<0s^{2}\left(\Tr C\Tr C^{3}-(\Tr C^{2})^{2}\right)=\frac{1}{d}\Tr((ds)^{1/2}C)\cdot\frac{1}{d}\Tr((ds)^{3/2}C^3)-\left(\frac{1}{d}\Tr(dsC^2)\right)^{2}\to-1<0

almost surely, which proves (3). On the other hand, when s≳ds\gtrsim d we again have

d2​mini≠j⁡(Ai​j​Aj​i−|Bi​j|2)→1d^{2}\min_{i\neq j}(A_{ij}A_{ji}-|B_{ij}|^{2})\to 1 almost surely.

Therefore, it is enough to consider the condition C≥0C\geq 0 for PPT properties by Proposition 5.1. Now Proposition 5.5 (2) and (3), combined with Proposition 5.9, and 5.6, imply the assertions (4) and (5), respectively. ∎

Remark 5.11.

Note that in the case of CDUC and DOC channels, in the regime d→∞d\to\infty, s∼c​ds\sim cd where c>4c>4, we cannot prove exactly that Φ𝖢𝖣𝖴𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{CDUC}} and Φ𝖣𝖮𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{DOC}} are asymptotically PPT. This is due to the fact that the absence of negative support of the limiting measure of the partial transpositions of the respective Choi matrices does not exclude the absence of negative outliers. To reach the desired conclusion, one may show the strong convergence [HT05] of the random matrices to their corresponding limit. For the partial transpositions of Wishart random matrices, Aubrun [Aub12] computed very large moments of the random matrices in order to show the norm convergence, as we do in the proof of Proposition 5.6 for the last assertion in Theorem 5.10.

The next result describes the asymptotic behavior of computable cross norm or realignment criterion [CW03, Rud05] for (the Choi matrix of) random DOC channels. The realignment criterion is known to be, in general, incomparable to the PPT criterion. Its form for diagonal invariant bipartite matrices was derived in [SN21, Lemma 2.12], namely

ΦA,B,C(3)​ is entanglement breaking⟹∑i,j=1dAi​j−‖A‖1≥∑i≠j=1dmax⁡(|Bi​j|,|Ci​j|).\Phi_{A,B,C}^{(3)}\text{ is entanglement breaking}\implies\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}A_{ij}-\|A\|_{1}\geq\sum_{i\neq j=1}^{d}\max(|B_{ij}|,|C_{ij}|).

The result below can be interpreted as the fact the realignment criterion is weaker than the PPT criterion for random DOC channels, from a random perspective. Note that the same phenomenon was proven for random bipartite quantum states in [AN12].

Proposition 5.12.

In every regime s≳dts\gtrsim d^{t} for some constants t>0t>0 and d→∞d\to\infty , random DOC channels satisfy the realignment criterion almost surely,

∑i,j=1dAi​j−‖A‖1≥∑i≠j=1dmax⁡(|Bi​j|,|Ci​j|).\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}A_{ij}-\|A\|_{1}\geq\sum_{i\neq j=1}^{d}\max(|B_{ij}|,|C_{ij}|).

The same conclusion holds for random CDUC and DUC channels.

This follows from the three almost sure limits:

∎

We now turn to the entanglement breaking (EB) property for random DOC channels.

Under the regime s≳d2+ts\gtrsim d^{2+t} for some constants t>0t>0 and d→∞d\to\infty, the random DOC channel Φ𝖣𝖮𝖢\Phi_{\mathsf{DOC}} is almost surely entanglement breaking.

as d→∞d\to\infty.

Since channels having diagonal (conjugate) unitary covariance can be obtained from DOC channels by twirling, we have the following simple consequence of Theorem 5.13.

Corollary 5.14.

Under the same hypothesis as above, the same conclusion holds for random DUC and CDUC channels.

6. The PPT2 conjecture holds for random DOC channels

Originally motivated by the theory of quantum repeaters, the PPT2 conjecture is now a central open question in quantum information theory, with recent ramifications into operator theory and operator algebras. We recall below its statement.

Conjecture 6.1 ([Chr12, CMHW18]).

The composition of two arbitrary PPT quantum channels is entanglement breaking.

The conjecture holds trivially in dimension d=2d=2, and it has been shown to hold also in dimension d=3d=3 [CMHW18, CYT19]. A plethora of papers establish the conjecture in several restricted scenarios, or with weaker conclusions (such as the need to compose a PPT map with itself several times) [LG15, KMP17, RJP18, HRF20, GKS20, JY20]. Importantly for us, Collins, Yin, and Zhong showed [CYZ18] that two independent random quantum channels that are PPT satisfy the conjecture.

In the case of quantum channels with diagonal unitary symmetry, is has been shown in [SN22b] that any two (C)DUC channels satisfy the PPT2 conjecture. The question whether the same holds for DOC channels has been left open [SN22b, Conjecture 5.1]. In this section, we contribute to this conjecture in two perspectives: deterministic and random. First of all, we show that one of the conditions for two PPT (C)DUC channels in [SN22b] can be relaxed to DOC. Furthermore, we answer in the affirmative this question for random DOC channels, under much weaker conditions. We refer to Corollaries 6.4 and 6.5 for the details.

The results rely on the following condition for the composition of two matrix triples to be TCP. Recall from [SN21, Lemmas 9.3 and 9.7] that the composition of two DOC channels is DOC:

ΦA,B,C(3)∘ΦD,E,F(3)=Φ𝒜,ℬ,𝒞(3)\Phi^{(3)}_{A,B,C}\circ\Phi^{(3)}_{D,E,F}=\Phi^{(3)}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}}

with (𝒜,ℬ,𝒞):=(A,B,C)∘(D,E,F)(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}):=(A,B,C)\circ(D,E,F), where

𝒜\displaystyle\mathcal{A} =A​D,\displaystyle=AD,
ℬ\displaystyle\mathcal{B} =diag⁡(A​D)+B∘⊙E∘+C∘⊙F∘T,\displaystyle=\mathrm{diag}(AD)+\accentset{\circ}{B}\odot\accentset{\circ}{E}+\accentset{\circ}{C}\odot\accentset{\circ}{F}^{T},
𝒞\displaystyle\mathcal{C} =diag⁡(A​D)+B∘⊙F∘+C∘⊙E∘T.\displaystyle=\mathrm{diag}(AD)+\accentset{\circ}{B}\odot\accentset{\circ}{F}+\accentset{\circ}{C}\odot\accentset{\circ}{E}^{T}.
Proposition 6.2.

If (A,B,C)(A,B,C) and (D,E,F)(D,E,F) are triples of matrices such that the corresponding DOC linear maps ΦA,B,C(3)\Phi_{A,B,C}^{(3)}, ΦD,E,F(3)\Phi_{D,E,F}^{(3)} are completely positive, and, moreover, for all i≠j∈[d]i\neq j\in[d],

(19) (Ai​i​Di​id−1+Ai​j​Dj​i)​(Aj​j​Dj​jd−1+Aj​i​Di​j)\displaystyle\left(\frac{A_{ii}D_{ii}}{d-1}+A_{ij}D_{ji}\right)\left(\frac{A_{jj}D_{jj}}{d-1}+A_{ji}D_{ij}\right) ≥max⁡(|Bi​j​Ei​j+Ci​j​Fi​j¯|2,|Bi​j​Fi​j+Ci​j​Ei​j¯|2),\displaystyle\geq\max(|B_{ij}E_{ij}+C_{ij}\overline{F_{ij}}|^{2},|B_{ij}F_{ij}+C_{ij}\overline{E_{ij}}|^{2}),
(20) (A​D)i​j​(A​D)j​i\displaystyle(AD)_{ij}(AD)_{ji} ≥max⁡(|Bi​j​Ei​j+Ci​j​Fi​j¯|2,|Bi​j​Fi​j+Ci​j​Ei​j¯|2).\displaystyle\geq\max(|B_{ij}E_{ij}+C_{ij}\overline{F_{ij}}|^{2},|B_{ij}F_{ij}+C_{ij}\overline{E_{ij}}|^{2}).

Then, their composition (A,B,C)∘(D,E,F)(A,B,C)\circ(D,E,F) is TCP.

Proof.

The proof is a slight modification of the proof of [SN22b, Theorem 4.5] in straightforward way. Using the notation in Eq. 18, we can decompose (𝒜,ℬ,𝒞)=∑1≤i<j≤d(𝒜(i​j),ℬ(i​j),𝒞(i​j))(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq d}(\mathcal{A}^{(ij)},\mathcal{B}^{(ij)},\mathcal{C}^{(ij)}) where
