ℬ(i​j)\displaystyle\mathcal{B}^{(ij)} =(1d−1​Ai​i​Di​i+Ai​j​Dj​iBi​j​Ei​j+Ci​j​Fi​j¯Bj​i​Ej​i+Cj​i​Fj​i¯1d−1​Aj​j​Dj​j+Aj​i​Di​j)i,j∈[d],\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{1}{d-1}A_{ii}D_{ii}+A_{ij}D_{ji}&B_{ij}E_{ij}+C_{ij}\overline{F_{ij}}\\ B_{ji}E_{ji}+C_{ji}\overline{F_{ji}}&\frac{1}{d-1}A_{jj}D_{jj}+A_{ji}D_{ij}\end{pmatrix}_{i,j\in[d]},
𝒞(i​j)\displaystyle\mathcal{C}^{(ij)} =(1d−1​Ai​i​Di​i+Ai​j​Dj​iBi​j​Fi​j+Ci​j​Ei​j¯Bj​i​Fj​i+Cj​i​Ej​i¯1d−1​Aj​j​Dj​j+Aj​i​Di​j)i,j∈[d],\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{1}{d-1}A_{ii}D_{ii}+A_{ij}D_{ji}&B_{ij}F_{ij}+C_{ij}\overline{E_{ij}}\\ B_{ji}F_{ji}+C_{ji}\overline{E_{ji}}&\frac{1}{d-1}A_{jj}D_{jj}+A_{ji}D_{ij}\end{pmatrix}_{i,j\in[d]},

since ET=E¯E^{T}=\overline{E} and FT=F¯F^{T}=\overline{F}. The two conditions (19) and (20), combined with Proposition 5.1, guarantee that each triple (𝒜(i​j),ℬ(i​j),𝒞(i​j))(\mathcal{A}^{(ij)},\mathcal{B}^{(ij)},\mathcal{C}^{(ij)}) is a “PPT” triple in 22-dimensional space, and hence TCP. This shows that (𝒜,ℬ,𝒞)(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}) is TCP. ∎

Remark 6.3.

We actually show something stronger: the composition has factor width 2, see [SN22b, Definition 3.2]:

(A,B,C)∘(D,E,F)∈𝖳𝖢𝖯d(2).(A,B,C)\circ(D,E,F)\in\mathsf{TCP}_{d}^{(2)}.

Note that the conditions Eqs. 19 and 20 are already weak enough to improve the main result of [SN22b, Theorem 4.5]. Indeed, suppose that ΦA,B,C(3)\Phi^{(3)}_{A,B,C} and ΦD,E,F(3)\Phi^{(3)}_{D,E,F} are PPT, and that one of BB, CC, EE, or FF is diagonal (corresponding to either ΦA,B,C(3)\Phi^{(3)}_{A,B,C} or ΦD,E,F(3)\Phi^{(3)}_{D,E,F} being DUC / CDUC). Then by Proposition 5.1 we have the entrywise inequalities

Ai​j​Aj​i≥max⁡(|Bi​j|2,|Ci​j|2),Di​j​Dj​i≥max⁡(|Ei​j|2,|Fi​j|2),i≠j∈[d],A_{ij}A_{ji}\geq\max(|B_{ij}|^{2},|C_{ij}|^{2}),\quad D_{ij}D_{ji}\geq\max(|E_{ij}|^{2},|F_{ij}|^{2}),\quad i\neq j\in[d],

which yields Eq. 19 since any of the diagonal conditions imply that

max⁡(|Bi​j​Ei​j+Ci​j​Fi​j¯|2,|Bi​j​Fi​j+Ci​j​Ei​j¯|2)≤max⁡(|Bi​j​Ei​j|2,|Ci​j​Fi​j¯|2,|Bi​j​Fi​j|2,|Ci​j​Ei​j¯|2).\max(|B_{ij}E_{ij}+C_{ij}\overline{F_{ij}}|^{2},|B_{ij}F_{ij}+C_{ij}\overline{E_{ij}}|^{2})\leq\max(|B_{ij}E_{ij}|^{2},|C_{ij}\overline{F_{ij}}|^{2},|B_{ij}F_{ij}|^{2},|C_{ij}\overline{E_{ij}}|^{2}).

Furthermore, Eq. 20 holds since Φ𝒜,ℬ,𝒞(3)=ΦA,B,C(3)∘ΦD,E,F(3)\Phi^{(3)}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}}=\Phi^{(3)}_{A,B,C}\circ\Phi^{(3)}_{D,E,F} is PPT. Consequently, (𝒜,ℬ,𝒞)∈𝖳𝖢𝖯d(2)(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\in\mathsf{TCP}_{d}^{(2)}, and hence Φ𝒜,ℬ,𝒞(3)\Phi^{(3)}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}} is entanglement breaking. We summarize the argument in the following corollary.

Corollary 6.4.

If ΦA,B,C(3)\Phi_{A,B,C}^{(3)} and ΦD,E(i)\Phi_{D,E}^{(i)} (i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}) are both PPT maps, then both compositions ΦA,B,C(3)∘ΦD,E(i)\Phi_{A,B,C}^{(3)}\circ\Phi_{D,E}^{(i)} and ΦD,E(i)∘ΦA,B,C(3)\Phi_{D,E}^{(i)}\circ\Phi_{A,B,C}^{(3)} are entanglement breaking.

The conditions in Proposition 5.1 also allow us to obtain another main result for random DOC channels.

Theorem 6.5.

Consider two random DOC channels Φi∼μd,si𝖣𝖮𝖢\Phi_{i}\sim\mu^{\mathsf{DOC}}_{d,s_{i}}, i=1,2i=1,2, in the asymptotic regime where d→∞d\to\infty and si≳dtis_{i}\gtrsim d^{t_{i}} for some constants ti>0t_{i}>0. Then almost surely as d→∞d\to\infty, the composition Φ1∘Φ2\Phi_{1}\circ\Phi_{2} is entanglement breaking.

In particular, in the asymptotic regime above, any two random DOC channels satisfy the PPT2 conjecture.

Let Φ1=ΦA,B,C(3)\Phi_{1}=\Phi_{A,B,C}^{(3)} and Φ2=ΦD,E,F(3)\Phi_{2}=\Phi_{D,E,F}^{(3)}. The result follows from Proposition 6.2 and Proposition 5.9: almost surely, we have

limd→∞d4​mini≠j⁡(Ai​i​Di​id−1+Ai​j​Dj​i)​(Aj​j​Dj​jd−1+Aj​i​Di​j)=1,\lim_{d\to\infty}d^{4}\min_{i\neq j}\left(\frac{A_{ii}D_{ii}}{d-1}+A_{ij}D_{ji}\right)\left(\frac{A_{jj}D_{jj}}{d-1}+A_{ji}D_{ij}\right)=1,

while d4​maxi≠j​|Bi​j​Ei​j+Ci​j​Fi​j¯|2→0d^{4}\max_{i\neq j}|B_{ij}E_{ij}+C_{ij}\overline{F_{ij}}|^{2}\to 0 and d4​maxi≠j​|Bi​j​Fi​j+Ci​j​Ei​j¯|2→0d^{4}\max_{i\neq j}|B_{ij}F_{ij}+C_{ij}\overline{E_{ij}}|^{2}\to 0. Therefore, the conditions (19) and (20) hold asymptotically. ∎

Remark 6.6.

We would like to emphasize that the hypothesis of Theorem 6.5 are very weak:

  • •

    The two channels need not be PPT; actually, from Theorem 5.10, if si∼ci​dtis_{i}\sim c_{i}d^{t_{i}} with 0<ti<10<t_{i}<1 and ci>0c_{i}>0, or ti=1t_{i}=1 and ci<4c_{i}<4, Φi\Phi_{i} is asymptotically not PPT.

  • •

    There is no assumption whatsoever about the correlations of the two random variables Φ1\Phi_{1} and Φ2\Phi_{2}: the two DOC channels can be independent, equal, complex conjugate to one another, or have any possible correlation.

The fact that we can show that the PPT2 conjecture holds for random DOC quantum channels under such weak conditions (compared to [CYZ18] where the channels are assumed to be PPT and independent) is due to the presence of the 𝒟​𝒪d\mathcal{DO}_{d} covariance.

Appendix A Technical lemmas and proofs

We gather in this appendix some technical background material, as well as the proofs of some of the results in the main text.

A.1. General results about the combinatorics of permutations and Weingarten functions

Our main approach to understanding the entanglement properties of the different models of random covariant channels is the moment method in random matrix theory. Specifically, we shall apply graphical Weingarten calculus [Col03, CŚ06, CN10] to compute many kinds of integrals involving Haar random isometries for the precise analysis. In this section, we introduce basic notions on permutations, partitions, and the Weingarten formula. Moreover, we present several combinatorial lemmas which will be useful throughout the appendix for the actual computation later on.

The main combinatorial objects that appear in the resolution of integrals with respect to the Haar measure on the unitary group are permutations and, in the limit of large dimensions, non-crossing partitions. We refer the reader to the excellent collection of lecture notes [NS06] for an introduction to the relation between these concepts, free probability theory, and random matrix theory.

We shall denote by SpS_{p} the symmetric group of order pp, that is the permutations of the set

[p]:={1,2,…,p}.[p]:=\{1,2,\ldots,p\}.

For a permutation α∈Sp\alpha\in S_{p}, we denote by #​α\#\alpha the number of cycles in its cycle decomposition, including singletons. We have #​id=p\#\mathrm{id}=p, whereas for the full cycle permutation #​γ=1\#\gamma=1, were

γ:=(pp−1⋯ 3 2 1)∈Sp.\gamma:=(p\;\;p-1\,\cdots\,3\;2\;1)\in S_{p}.

The length |α||\alpha| of a permutation α∈Sp\alpha\in S_{p} is the minimal number of transpositions that multiply to α\alpha. We have the important relation [NS06, Proposition 23.11]

∀α∈Sp,#​α+|α|=p.\forall\alpha\in S_{p},\qquad\#\alpha+|\alpha|=p.

Let us discuss now the Weingarten formula [Col03, CŚ06], the main technical tool that will allow us to compute various average quantities related to the Haar measure on the set of isometries. Below, the integral is taken either to the Haar measure on the set of isometries V:ℂk→ℂdV:\mathbb{C}^{k}\to\mathbb{C}^{d} for k≤dk\leq d. The isometry VV can be thought of as the truncation (keeping the first kk columns) of a Haar-distributed random unitary matrix U∈𝒰dU\in\mathcal{U}_{d}.

Theorem A.1.

Then

(21) ∫Vi1​j1⋯Vip​jpV¯i1′​j1′⋯V¯ip′​jp′dV=∑σ,τ∈Spδi1​iσ⁡(1)′…δip​iσ⁡(p)′δj1​jτ⁡(1)′…δjp​jτ⁡(p)′Wgd(τσ−1).\int V_{i_{1}j_{1}}\cdots V_{i_{p}j_{p}}\overline{V}_{i^{\prime}_{1}j^{\prime}_{1}}\cdots\overline{V}_{i^{\prime}_{p}j^{\prime}_{p}}\,\mathrm{d}V=\sum_{\sigma,\tau\in S_{p}}\delta_{i_{1}i^{\prime}_{\sigma(1)}}\ldots\delta_{i_{p}i^{\prime}_{\sigma(p)}}\delta_{j_{1}j^{\prime}_{\tau(1)}}\ldots\delta_{j_{p}j^{\prime}_{\tau(p)}}\operatorname{Wg}_{d}(\tau\sigma^{-1}).

Lemma A.4.
  1. (1)

    Let us write the power series expansion

    s1−p(s+1)⋯(s+p−1)=∑k=0∞ak,ps−ks^{1-p}(s+1)\cdots(s+p-1)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_{k,p}s^{-k}

    in s−1s^{-1}. Then for each kk, the coefficient ak,pa_{k,p} is a polynomial in pp of degree 2​k2k. Moreover, ak,p=0a_{k,p}=0 for all k≥pk\geq p.

  2. (2)

    If we write the power series expansion

    ∑α∈𝒫1,2​(p)s−|α|=∑k=0∞bk,p​s−k,\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal{P}_{1,2}(p)}s^{-|\alpha|}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}b_{k,p}s^{-k},

    then b0,p≡1b_{0,p}\equiv 1 and bk,p=p(p−1)⋯(p−2k+1)2k​k!b_{k,p}=\frac{p(p-1)\cdots(p-2k+1)}{2^{k}k!} for k≥1k\geq 1.

  3. (3)

    If we write the power series expansion

    then c0,p≡1c_{0,p}\equiv 1 and ck,p=(p2​k)​Catk=p(p−1)⋯(p−2k+1)(k+1)!​k!c_{k,p}=\binom{p}{2k}{\rm Cat}_{k}=\frac{p(p-1)\cdots(p-2k+1)}{(k+1)!k!} for k≥1k\geq 1.

Proof.

(1) The second assertion is obvious since s(s+1)⋯(s+p−1)s(s+1)\cdots(s+p-1) is a polynomial in ss of degree pp with zero constant. On the other hand, we can easily see that a0,p≡1a_{0,p}\equiv 1, and ak,pa_{k,p} satisfy the recurrence

ak,p=(p−1)​ak−1,p−1+ak,p−1,p≥1,k≥1,a_{k,p}=(p-1)a_{k-1,p-1}+a_{k,p-1},\;\;p\geq 1,k\geq 1,

from the relation

s(s+1)⋯(s+p−1)=sp∑k=0∞ak,ps−k=(s+p−1)sp−1∑k=0∞ak,p−1s−k.s(s+1)\cdots(s+p-1)=s^{p}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_{k,p}s^{-k}=(s+p-1)s^{p-1}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_{k,p-1}s^{-k}.

Therefore, we have ak,p=∑j=0p−1j​ak−1,j+ak,0=∑j=0p−1j​ak−1,ja_{k,p}=\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}ja_{k-1,j}+a_{k,0}=\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}ja_{k-1,j}. By induction hypothesis, p​ak−1,ppa_{k-1,p} is a polynomial in pp of degree 2​k−12k-1, and hence the first assertion follows.

(2) We leave its proof to the reader, just by noting that bk,pb_{k,p} is equal to the number of permutations consisting of exactly kk transpositions (and p−2​kp-2k singletons) in their cycles.

(3) Similarly with (2), ck,pc_{k,p} is the number of permutations consisting of kk transpositions which are non-crossing. We can find this by first choosing 2​k2k elements in [p][p] and then count the number of non-crossing pair partitions (=Catk={\rm Cat}_{k}) of these elements. ∎

Lemma A.5.

Given two permutations σ1,σ2∈Sp\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\in S_{p}, the map

Sp∋α↦(|σ1−1​α|+|α−1​σ2|)​mod​ 2∈{0,1}S_{p}\ni\alpha\mapsto(|\sigma_{1}^{-1}\alpha|+|\alpha^{-1}\sigma_{2}|)\;{\rm mod\,}2\in\{0,1\}

is constant. In particular, for all α∈Sp\alpha\in S_{p}, there exists a nonnegative integer gg such that

|σ1−1​α|+|α−1​σ2|=|σ1−1​σ2|+2​g.|\sigma_{1}^{-1}\alpha|+|\alpha^{-1}\sigma_{2}|=|\sigma_{1}^{-1}\sigma_{2}|+2g.
Proof.

The first assertion follows from the observations that every permutation α\alpha can be written as a product of transpositions and |σ​τ|=|σ|±1|\sigma\tau|=|\sigma|\pm 1 for every σ∈Sp\sigma\in S_{p} and a transposition τ\tau [NS06, Lemma 23.10]. The second point then follows from the first point and the triangle inequality |σ1−1​α|+|α−1​σ2|≥|σ1−1​σ2||\sigma_{1}^{-1}\alpha|+|\alpha^{-1}\sigma_{2}|\geq|\sigma_{1}^{-1}\sigma_{2}|. ∎

We shall denote by 𝒫⁡(p)\mathcal{P}(p) the set of partitions of [p]={1,2,…,p}[p]=\{1,2,\ldots,p\}. Importantly, we denote by N​C​(p)NC(p) the set of non-crossing partitions of [p][p], that is partitions π\pi for which there do not exist i<j<k<l∈[p]i<j<k<l\in[p] such that i∼πki\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\sim}}k and j∼πlj\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\sim}}l (in which case we say that the blocks of π\pi containing ii and kk and, respectively, jj and ll are crossing). Let us denote by SN​C​(σ):={α∈Sp:|α|+|α−1​σ|=|σ|}S_{NC}(\sigma):=\{\alpha\in S_{p}:|\alpha|+|\alpha^{-1}\sigma|=|\sigma|\} the set of permutations which lie on a geodesic from id\mathrm{id} to σ\sigma. In what follows, we will provide a complete description of the elements of SN​C​(σ)S_{NC}(\sigma) for arbitrary permutation σ∈Sp\sigma\in S_{p}. First, we introduce the projection map π:Sp→𝒫⁡(p)\pi:S_{p}\to\mathcal{P}(p) which naturally identifies each of the cycles of a permutation α\alpha as blocks of π⁡(α)\pi(\alpha). Then the following proposition states that we can interpret the elements of SN​C​(γ)S_{NC}(\gamma) as non-crossing partitions when γ\gamma is a full cycle.

Proposition A.6 ([NS06, Proposition 23.23]).

Let γ=(pp−1⋯ 1)∈Sp\gamma=(p\;\;p-1\,\cdots\,1)\in S_{p}. Then the restriction map π|SN​C​(γ)\pi\bigm|_{S_{NC}(\gamma)} of the projection map π:Sp→𝒫⁡(p)\pi:S_{p}\to\mathcal{P}(p) defines a natural bijection between SN​C​(γ)S_{NC}(\gamma) and N​C​(p)NC(p), which preserves the partial order structure. More explicitely,

  1. (1)

    α∈SN​C​(γ)\alpha\in S_{NC}(\gamma) if and only if π⁡(α)\pi(\alpha) forms a non-crossing partition and every cycle of α\alpha can be written in the form

    (j1j2⋯jr),j1>j2>⋯>jr,(j_{1}\,j_{2}\,\cdots\,j_{r}),\quad j_{1}>j_{2}>\cdots>j_{r},
  2. (2)

    if α∈SN​C​(γ)\alpha\in S_{NC}(\gamma) and β∈SN​C​(α)\beta\in S_{NC}(\alpha), then β∈SN​C​(γ)\beta\in S_{NC}(\gamma) and π⁡(β)≤π⁡(α)\pi(\beta)\leq\pi(\alpha) as partitions [NS06, Definition 9.14].

Proposition A.7.

Let σ=c1⋯ck\sigma=c_{1}\cdots c_{k} be the cycle decomposition of σ∈Sp\sigma\in S_{p}. If α∈SN​C​(σ)\alpha\in S_{NC}(\sigma), then α\alpha can be decomposed into disjoint permutations α1⋯αk\alpha_{1}\cdots\alpha_{k} such that, for each i=1,…​ki=1,\ldots k, αi≤ci\alpha_{i}\leq c_{i} as partitions and αi∈SN​C​(ci)\alpha_{i}\in S_{NC}(c_{i}). Furthermore, if α′∈SN​C​(σ)\alpha^{\prime}\in S_{NC}(\sigma) and α≡α′\alpha\equiv\alpha^{\prime} as partitions, then α=α′\alpha=\alpha^{\prime} as permutations.

Proof.

By re-indexing (i.e. conjugation δ​σ​δ−1\delta\sigma\delta^{-1} for some δ∈Sp\delta\in S_{p}), we may assume that

ci=(pi(pi−1)⋯(pi−1+1)),i=1,…,k,c_{i}=(p_{i}\,\,(p_{i}-1)\,\cdots\,(p_{i-1}+1)),\quad i=1,\ldots,k,

for some 1=p0<p1<⋯<pk=p.1=p_{0}<p_{1}<\cdots<p_{k}=p. Then Proposition A.6 implies that σ,α∈SN​C​(γ)\sigma,\alpha\in S_{NC}(\gamma) and α≤σ\alpha\leq\sigma as partitions. In particular, each block Vi={pi−1+1,…,pi−1,pi}V_{i}=\{p_{i-1}+1,\ldots,p_{i}-1,p_{i}\} is invariant under α\alpha, so the restriction αi:=α|Vi∈S⁡(Vi)\alpha_{i}:=\alpha\bigm|_{V_{i}}\in S(V_{i}) is well-defined. Now we can write α=α1⋯αk\alpha=\alpha_{1}\cdots\alpha_{k} and |α|=∑i=1k|αi||\alpha|=\sum_{i=1}^{k}|\alpha_{i}|. Moreover, the condition α∈SN​C​(σ)\alpha\in S_{NC}(\sigma) implies that

|σ|=∑i=1k|σi|≤∑i=1k(|αi|+|αi−1​σi|)=∑i|αi|+∑i|σi−1​αi|=|α|+|α−1​σ|=|σ|,|\sigma|=\sum_{i=1}^{k}|\sigma_{i}|\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k}(|\alpha_{i}|+|\alpha_{i}^{-1}\sigma_{i}|)=\sum_{i}|\alpha_{i}|+\sum_{i}|\sigma_{i}^{-1}\alpha_{i}|=|\alpha|+|\alpha^{-1}\sigma|=|\sigma|,

and therefore, the equality condition forces that αi∈SN​C​(σi)\alpha_{i}\in S_{NC}(\sigma_{i}) for all ii. Finally, the last statement follows from Proposition A.6(1): α,α′∈SN​C​(γ)\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}\in S_{NC}(\gamma) and π⁡(α)=π⁡(α′)\pi(\alpha)=\pi(\alpha^{\prime}) imply that α=α′\alpha=\alpha^{\prime}. ∎

Proposition A.7 implies that we have the natural bijection

(22) SN​C(σ)≅SN​C(c1)×⋯×SN​C(ck).S_{NC}(\sigma)\cong S_{NC}(c_{1})\times\cdots\times S_{NC}(c_{k}).

Now let us denote by SN​C1,2​(σ)S_{NC_{1,2}}(\sigma) the set of permutations in SN​C​(σ)S_{NC}(\sigma) having only cycles of size 1 or 2. The set can be defined equivalently by

(23) α∈SN​C1,2​(σ)⇔α∈SN​C​(σ)​ and ​α=α−1⇔α,α−1∈SN​C​(σ).\alpha\in S_{NC_{1,2}}(\sigma)\iff\alpha\in S_{NC}(\sigma)\text{ and }\alpha=\alpha^{-1}\iff\alpha,\alpha^{-1}\in S_{NC}(\sigma).

since any cycle having size larger than 2 is distinct from its inverse, and since α,α−1∈SN​C​(σ)\alpha,\alpha^{-1}\in S_{NC}(\sigma) implies α=α−1\alpha=\alpha^{-1} by Proposition A.7. Furthermore, note that the set SN​C1,2​(γ)S_{NC_{1,2}}(\gamma) can be identified with N​C1,2​(p)NC_{1,2}(p), the set of non-crossing partitions having only blocks of size 1 or 2, in a trivial way. Finally, if σ=c1⋯ck\sigma=c_{1}\cdots c_{k} is the cycle decomposition of σ\sigma, then the bijection Eq. 22 reduces to

(24) SN​C1,2(σ)≅SN​C1,2(c1)×⋯×SN​C1,2(ck).S_{NC_{1,2}}(\sigma)\cong S_{NC_{1,2}}(c_{1})\times\cdots\times S_{NC_{1,2}}(c_{k}).

For two partitions π1,π2∈𝒫⁡(p)\pi_{1},\pi_{2}\in\mathcal{P}(p), the join π1∨π2\pi_{1}\vee\pi_{2} is defined as the supremum of π1\pi_{1} and π2\pi_{2} in 𝒫⁡(p)\mathcal{P}(p) [NS06, Definition 9.15]. Since the length function |α|=p−#​α|\alpha|=p-\#\,\alpha only depends on the corresponding partition π⁡(α)\pi(\alpha), we can define |α∨β|:=p−#⁡(π⁡(α)∨π⁡(β))|\alpha\vee\beta|:=p-\#(\pi(\alpha)\vee\pi(\beta)) for arbitrary permutations α,β∈Sp\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}. Note that |α∨β|≥max⁡(|α|,|β|)|\alpha\vee\beta|\geq\max(|\alpha|,|\beta|) in general since the join operation ∨\vee does not increase the number of blocks as partitions. Moreover, if |α∨β|=|α|=|β||\alpha\vee\beta|=|\alpha|=|\beta|, or equivalently #⁡(π⁡(α)∨π⁡(β))=#⁡(π⁡(α))=#⁡(π⁡(β))\#(\pi(\alpha)\vee\pi(\beta))=\#(\pi(\alpha))=\#(\pi(\beta)), then we have π⁡(α)=π⁡(β)\pi(\alpha)=\pi(\beta).

We now present several permutation inequalities that will be applied later to prove Proposition 5.5.

Lemma A.8.

Let σ∈Sp\sigma\in S_{p} be a permutation.

  1. (1)

    For all α,β∈Sp\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}, we have

    |α|+2​|α​β−1|+|(σ−1​α)∨(σ−1​β−1)|≥|σ|,|\alpha|+2|\alpha\beta^{-1}|+|(\sigma^{-1}\alpha)\vee(\sigma^{-1}\beta^{-1})|\geq|\sigma|,

    and the equality holds if and only if α=β∈SN​C1,2​(σ)\alpha=\beta\in S_{NC_{1,2}}(\sigma). Furthermore, whenever the equality does not hold, we have

    |α|+2​|α​β−1|+|(σ−1​α)∨(σ−1​β−1)|≥|σ|+2.|\alpha|+2|\alpha\beta^{-1}|+|(\sigma^{-1}\alpha)\vee(\sigma^{-1}\beta^{-1})|\geq|\sigma|+2.
  2. (2)

    For all α,β∈Sp\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}, we have

    |α​β−1|+|(σ−1​α)∨(σ−1​β−1)|≥12​|σ2|,|\alpha\beta^{-1}|+|(\sigma^{-1}\alpha)\vee(\sigma^{-1}\beta^{-1})|\geq\frac{1}{2}|\sigma^{2}|,

    and the equality holds if and only if α=β∈SN​C1,2​(σ)\alpha=\beta\in S_{NC_{1,2}}(\sigma) and σ−1​α∈SN​C​(σ−2)\sigma^{-1}\alpha\in S_{NC}(\sigma^{-2}). Furthermore, when σ=γ=(pp−1⋯ 1)\sigma=\gamma=(p\;\;p-1\,\cdots\,1), α∈N​C1,2​(p)\alpha\in NC_{1,2}(p) is ‘maximally paired’, i.e.,

    (25) p=even\displaystyle p=\text{even} ⟹α consists of p2 transpositions i.e., α∈N​C2​(p),\displaystyle\implies\text{$\alpha$ consists of $\frac{p}{2}$ transpositions i.e., $\alpha\in NC_{2}(p)$},
    (26) p=odd\displaystyle p=\text{odd} ⟹α consists of one singleton and p−12 transpositions.\displaystyle\implies\text{$\alpha$ consists of one singleton and $\frac{p-1}{2}$ transpositions}.
Proof.

(1) Since |(σ−1​α)∨(σ−1​β−1)|≥max⁡(|σ−1​α|,|σ−1​β−1|)|(\sigma^{-1}\alpha)\vee(\sigma^{-1}\beta^{-1})|\geq\max(|\sigma^{-1}\alpha|,|\sigma^{-1}\beta^{-1}|), we have

LHS\displaystyle{\rm LHS} ≥|α|+|σ−1​α|≥|σ|,\displaystyle\geq|\alpha|+|\sigma^{-1}\alpha|\geq|\sigma|,
LHS\displaystyle{\rm LHS} ≥|α|+|α​β−1|+|σ−1​β−1|≥|α−1|+|σ−1​α−1|≥|σ|.\displaystyle\geq|\alpha|+|\alpha\beta^{-1}|+|\sigma^{-1}\beta^{-1}|\geq|\alpha^{-1}|+|\sigma^{-1}\alpha^{-1}|\geq|\sigma|.

In particular, the equality conditions for both two inequalities imply that α=β\alpha=\beta and α,α−1∈SN​C​(σ)\alpha,\alpha^{-1}\in S_{NC}(\sigma), and therefore α∈SN​C1,2\alpha\in S_{NC_{1,2}} by Eq. 23. On the other hand, if the equality does not hold, then either α≠β\alpha\neq\beta or α=β∉SN​C1,2\alpha=\beta\not\in S_{NC_{1,2}}. For the former case, we have

LHS≥(|α|+|σ−1​α|)+2​|α​β−1|≥|σ|+2,{\rm LHS}\geq(|\alpha|+|\sigma^{-1}\alpha|)+2|\alpha\beta^{-1}|\geq|\sigma|+2,

and for the latter case, we again have

LHS≥max⁡(|α|+|σ−1​α|,|α−1|+|σ−1​α−1|)≥|σ|+2{\rm LHS}\geq\max(|\alpha|+|\sigma^{-1}\alpha|,|\alpha^{-1}|+|\sigma^{-1}\alpha^{-1}|)\geq|\sigma|+2

by Lemma A.5.

(2) Similarly as above, we have

LHS≥|α​β−1|+max⁡(|σ−1​α|,|σ−1​β−1|)≥12​(|α​β−1|+(|σ−1​α|+|α−1​β|+|β−1​σ−1|))≥12​|σ2|.{\rm LHS}\geq|\alpha\beta^{-1}|+\max(|\sigma^{-1}\alpha|,|\sigma^{-1}\beta^{-1}|)\geq\frac{1}{2}\Big(|\alpha\beta^{-1}|+(|\sigma^{-1}\alpha|+|\alpha^{-1}\beta|+|\beta^{-1}\sigma^{-1}|)\Big)\geq\frac{1}{2}|\sigma^{2}|.

All the equalities above hold if and only if α=β\alpha=\beta, σ−1​α≡σ−1​α−1\sigma^{-1}\alpha\equiv\sigma^{-1}\alpha^{-1} as partitions, and |σ−1​α|+|σ−1​α−1|=|σ−2||\sigma^{-1}\alpha|+|\sigma^{-1}\alpha^{-1}|=|\sigma^{-2}|. Note that the last condition implies that σ−1​α,σ−1​α−1∈SN​C​(σ−2)\sigma^{-1}\alpha,\sigma^{-1}\alpha^{-1}\in S_{NC}(\sigma^{-2}), and therefore, α=α−1\alpha=\alpha^{-1} by Proposition A.7. In particular, every cycle of α\alpha has size 1 or 2.

We claim that α∈SN​C1,2​(σ)\alpha\in S_{NC_{1,2}}(\sigma) in this case. Indeed, by considering the cycle decomposition of σ\sigma and applying Proposition A.7 for σ−1​α∈SN​C​(σ−2)\sigma^{-1}\alpha\in S_{NC}(\sigma^{-2}), we may assume that σ=γ=(pp−1⋯ 1)\sigma=\gamma=(p\;\;p-1\,\cdots\,1). Then we have

|γ−1​α|=|γ−1​α−1|=12​|γ−2|={p/2−1if p is even,(p−1)/2if p is odd.|\gamma^{-1}\alpha|=|\gamma^{-1}\alpha^{-1}|=\frac{1}{2}|\gamma^{-2}|=\begin{cases}p/2-1&\text{if $p$ is even,}\\ (p-1)/2&\text{if $p$ is odd.}\end{cases}

Therefore, it suffices to show |α|={p/2if p is even,(p−1)/2if p is odd|\alpha|=\begin{cases}p/2&\text{if $p$ is even},\\ (p-1)/2&\text{if $p$ is odd}\end{cases} to conclude α∈SN​C1,2​(γ)≅N​C1,2​(p)\alpha\in S_{NC_{1,2}}(\gamma)\cong NC_{1,2}(p), which is equivalent to Eqs. 25 and 26. First, when pp is even, we have

γ−2=(1 3⋯p−1)(2 4⋯p),\gamma^{-2}=(1\,3\,\cdots p-1)(2\,4\,\cdots p),

and in particular, the condition γ−1​α∈SN​C​(γ−2)\gamma^{-1}\alpha\in S_{NC}(\gamma^{-2}) implies that every cycle γ−1​α\gamma^{-1}\alpha consists of the elements having the same parity. This is impossible when there is any i∈[p]i\in[p] such that α⁡(i)=i\alpha(i)=i. Therefore, we have Eq. 25. On the other hand, when pp is odd, we can write

γ−2=(1  3⋯p  2  4⋯p−1).\gamma^{-2}=(1\,\,3\,\,\cdots\,\,p\,\,2\,\,4\cdots\,\,p-1).

If Eq. 26 is not true, then we have at least three singletons inside α\alpha, and in particular, we can find two distinct integers i<i′i<i^{\prime} with the same parity such that α⁡(i)=i\alpha(i)=i and α⁡(i′)=i′\alpha(i^{\prime})=i^{\prime}. Then γ−1​α​(i)=i+1\gamma^{-1}\alpha(i)=i+1, γ−1​α​(i′)=i′+1\gamma^{-1}\alpha(i^{\prime})=i^{\prime}+1, and we can easily see that the pairs (i,i+1)(i,i+1) and (i′,i′+1)(i^{\prime},i^{\prime}+1) are crossing inside the full cycle γ−2\gamma^{-2}. Moreover, i,i+1,i′,i′+1i,i+1,i^{\prime},i^{\prime}+1 cannot appear, in this order, in the same cycle of γ−1​α\gamma^{-1}\alpha since any cycle inside γ−1​α∈SN​C​(γ−2)\gamma^{-1}\alpha\in S_{NC}(\gamma^{-2}) must be of the form

(i1⋯irj1⋯jr′)(i_{1}\,\cdots i_{r}\,j_{1}\,\cdots j_{r^{\prime}})

where i1<⋯<iri_{1}<\cdots<i_{r} are odd integers and j1<⋯<jr′j_{1}<\cdots<j_{r^{\prime}} are even integers, according to Proposition A.6 (1). Consequently, we have a contradiction, and hence Eq. 26 holds.

Lemma A.9.

Let γ:=(pp−1⋯ 1)∈Sp\gamma:=(p\,\,p-1\,\cdots\,1)\in S_{p} and γ~:=(pp−1⋯ 1)(2p 2p−1⋯p+1)∈S2​p\tilde{\gamma}:=(p\,\,p-1\,\cdots\,1)(2p\;2p-1\,\cdots\,p+1)\in S_{2p}. For p=2,3p=2,3 we have

(27) α,β∈Sp,|α|+|α​β−1|>p2\displaystyle\alpha,\beta\in S_{p},\;\;|\alpha|+|\alpha\beta^{-1}|>\frac{p}{2} ⟹|γ−1​α∨γ−1​β−1|+|α​β−1|≥p2+12,\displaystyle\implies|\gamma^{-1}\alpha\vee\gamma^{-1}\beta^{-1}|+|\alpha\beta^{-1}|\geq\frac{p}{2}+\frac{1}{2},
(28) α,β∈S2​p,|α|+|α​β−1|>p\displaystyle\alpha,\beta\in S_{2p},\;\;|\alpha|+|\alpha\beta^{-1}|>p ⟹|γ~−1​α∨γ~−1​β−1|+|α​β−1|≥p.\displaystyle\implies|\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\alpha\vee\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\beta^{-1}|+|\alpha\beta^{-1}|\geq p.
Proof.

Let us first consider the case p=2p=2. The proof of Eq. 27 is simple: |α|+|α​β−1|>1|\alpha|+|\alpha\beta^{-1}|>1 holds only if α=(1 2)\alpha=(1\,2) and β=id\beta=\mathrm{id}, and |γ−1​α∨γ−1​β−1|+|α​β−1|=2|\gamma^{-1}\alpha\vee\gamma^{-1}\beta^{-1}|+|\alpha\beta^{-1}|=2 in this case. Regarding Eq. 28, note that we always have |γ~−1​α∨γ~−1​β−1|≥1|\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\alpha\vee\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\beta^{-1}|\geq 1: otherwise, α=β=γ~=(1 2)​(3 4)\alpha=\beta=\tilde{\gamma}=(1\,2)(3\,4), but this contradicts the condition |α|+|α​β−1|>2|\alpha|+|\alpha\beta^{-1}|>2. Now if we assume α=β\alpha=\beta and |γ~−1​α∨γ~−1​α−1|=1|\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\alpha\vee\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\alpha^{-1}|=1, then max⁡(|γ~−1​α|,|γ~−1​α−1|)=1\max(|\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\alpha|,|\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\alpha^{-1}|)=1. Both the cases |γ~−1​α|=0|\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\alpha|=0 and |γ~−1​α|=0|\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\alpha|=0 imply that α=β=γ~\alpha=\beta=\tilde{\gamma} for which we already had a contradiction. If |γ~−1​α|=|γ~−1​α−1|=1=|γ~−1​α∨γ~−1​α−1||\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\alpha|=|\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\alpha^{-1}|=1=|\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\alpha\vee\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\alpha^{-1}|, then we actually have γ~−1​α=γ~−1​α−1\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\alpha=\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\alpha^{-1} and α=α−1\alpha=\alpha^{-1}. This again induces a contradiction since |α|+|α​β−1|=|α|≤2|\alpha|+|\alpha\beta^{-1}|=|\alpha|\leq 2.

Now consider the case p=3p=3. By Lemma A.8 (2), we already know

|γ−1​α∨γ−1​β−1|+|α​β−1|\displaystyle|\gamma^{-1}\alpha\vee\gamma^{-1}\beta^{-1}|+|\alpha\beta^{-1}| ≥12​|γ2|=1\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}|\gamma^{2}|=1

for all α,β∈Sp\alpha,\beta\in S_{p} and the equality holds only if α=β\alpha=\beta and |α|=1|\alpha|=1 (Eq. 26) which does not satisfy |α|+|α​β−1|>3/2|\alpha|+|\alpha\beta^{-1}|>3/2. This implies Eq. 27. Similarly, we always have

|γ~−1​α∨γ~−1​β−1|+|α​β−1|\displaystyle|\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\alpha\vee\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\beta^{-1}|+|\alpha\beta^{-1}| ≥12​|γ~2|=2,\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}|\tilde{\gamma}^{2}|=2,

and the equality condition implies that α=β∈SN​C1,2​(γ~)\alpha=\beta\in S_{NC_{1,2}}(\tilde{\gamma}) and

|α|=|γ~|−|γ~−1​α|=|γ~|−12|γ~2|=2,|\alpha|=|\tilde{\gamma}|-|\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\alpha|=|\tilde{\gamma}|-\frac{1}{2}|\tilde{\gamma}^{2}|=2,

which contradicts the condition |α|+|α​β−1|>3|\alpha|+|\alpha\beta^{-1}|>3. This implies Eq. 28. ∎

Remark A.10.

By repeating the same arguments above, we can actually show that Eqs. 27 and 28 hold for all odd integers pp. However, they are not true for even p≥4p\geq 4 in general: when α=β=(1 2 3 4)∈S4\alpha=\beta=(1\,2\,3\,4)\in S_{4},

|γ−1​α∨γ−1​β−1|+|α​β−1|=|(1 3)​(2 4)|=2<52,|\gamma^{-1}\alpha\vee\gamma^{-1}\beta^{-1}|+|\alpha\beta^{-1}|=|(1\,3)(2\,4)|=2<\frac{5}{2},

and when α=β=(1 2 3 4)​(5 6)​(7 8)∈S8\alpha=\beta=(1\,2\,3\,4)(5\,6)(7\,8)\in S_{8},

|γ~−1​α∨γ~−1​β−1|+|α​β−1|=|(1 3)​(2 4)​(5 7)|=3<4.|\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\alpha\vee\tilde{\gamma}^{-1}\beta^{-1}|+|\alpha\beta^{-1}|=|(1\,3)(2\,4)(5\,7)|=3<4.

A.2. Scalar parameters

This section contains results about the real parameters λ1,2,3(d,s)\lambda_{1,2,3}^{(d,s)} which appear in the study of random (conjugate) unitary, orthogonal, and hyperoctahedral quantum channels from Sections 3 and 4.

The following moment formulae characterize the distributions of these random variables.

Lemma A.11.

The moments of the random variables λ1,2,3(d,s)\lambda_{1,2,3}^{(d,s)} are given by

𝔼⁡[(λ1(d,s))p]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}\big)^{p}\Big] =s(s+1)⋯(s+p−1)∑β∈Spd#​βWgd​s(β)\displaystyle=s(s+1)\cdots(s+p-1)\sum_{\beta\in S_{p}}d^{\#\beta}{\operatorname{Wg}}_{ds}(\beta)
𝔼⁡[(λ2(d,s))p]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(\lambda_{2}^{(d,s)}\big)^{p}\Big] =∑α,β∈Sps#​α​d#⁡(α​β)​Wgd​s⁡(α​β−1)\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}}s^{\#\alpha}d^{\#(\alpha\beta)}{\operatorname{Wg}}_{ds}(\alpha\beta^{-1})
𝔼⁡[(λ3(d,s))p]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(\lambda_{3}^{(d,s)}\big)^{p}\Big] =∑α,β∈Sps#​α​d#⁡(α∨β)​Wgd​s⁡(α​β−1).\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}}s^{\#\alpha}d^{\#(\alpha\vee\beta)}\operatorname{Wg}_{ds}(\alpha\beta^{-1}).
Proof.

To obtain the three formulas in the statement, we apply the graphical Weingarten formula for the diagram consisting of pp (disconnected) copies of the diagram for λ1,2,3(d,s)\lambda_{1,2,3}^{(d,s)} (see Figs. 3 and 6). In the case of λ1(d,s)\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}, we obtain

𝔼⁡[(λ1(d,s))p]=∑α,β∈Spd#⁡(α−1​β)​s#​α​Wgd​s⁡(α−1​β)=∑σ,π∈Spd#​π​s#​σ​Wgd​s⁡(π),\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}\big)^{p}\Big]=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}}d^{\#(\alpha^{-1}\beta)}s^{\#\alpha}\operatorname{Wg}_{ds}(\alpha^{-1}\beta)=\sum_{\sigma,\pi\in S_{p}}d^{\#\pi}s^{\#\sigma}\operatorname{Wg}_{ds}(\pi),

since there are precisely #⁡(α−1​β)\#(\alpha^{-1}\beta) loops of dimension dd and #​α\#\alpha loops of dimension ss. We use Lemma A.2 to compute explicitly the sum over σ\sigma.

Counting the loops in a similar fashion gives the formulas for λ2(d,s)\lambda_{2}^{(d,s)}. Regarding the integration of (λ3(d,s))p(\lambda_{3}^{(d,s)})^{p}, we can understand the diagram of λ3(d,s)\lambda_{3}^{(d,s)} by joining the two separated lines representing the tensor component of dimension dd as in Fig. 9. Note that after the graphical calculus in the diagram for α,β∈Sp\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}, the upper (external) and lower (internal) lines contributes #​α\#\,\alpha and #​β\#\,\beta loops of dimension dd, respectively. However, we have to “join” them because we identify the the two kinds of loops (thick lines in the figure). Consequently, all the blocks in α∨β\alpha\vee\beta contribute the same loop in the final diagram, and hence there are exactly #⁡(α∨β)\#(\alpha\vee\beta) loops of dimension dd. The term s#​αs^{\#\alpha} appears similarly with the case λ1,2(d,s)\lambda_{1,2}^{(d,s)}, and this concludes the proof.

∎

In the case s=1s=1, the random variable λ1(d,1)\lambda_{1}^{(d,1)} has an interesting interpretation. Indeed, in that case the random isometry VV is a Haar-distributed random unitary matrix U∈𝒰⁡(d)U\in\mathcal{U}(d), and thus

λ1(d,s=1)=|Tr⁡U|2.\lambda_{1}^{(d,s=1)}=|\Tr U|^{2}.

Then, for any p≤d/2p\leq d/2, we have [DS94, Theorem 2]

𝔼⁡[|Tr⁡U|2​p]=p!.\mathbb{E}\Big[\big|\Tr U\big|^{2p}\Big]=p!.

In the general case. if we apply graphical Weingarten formula and use the fact that σ↦Wgd⁡(σ)\sigma\mapsto\operatorname{Wg}_{d}(\sigma) is the pseudo-inverse of σ↦d#​σ\sigma\mapsto d^{\#\sigma} in ℂ⁡[Sp]\mathbb{C}[S_{p}], we can extend the same formula to all dd, and in general we have

𝔼⁡[|Tr⁡U|2​p]=p!​∑σ∈Spd#​σ​Wgd⁡(σ)=∑λ⊢p,l⁡(λ)≤ddλ2,\mathbb{E}\left[|\Tr U|^{2p}\right]=p!\sum_{\sigma\in S_{p}}d^{\#\sigma}\operatorname{Wg}_{d}(\sigma)=\sum_{\lambda\vdash p,\;l(\lambda)\leq d}d_{\lambda}^{2},

where dλd_{\lambda} is the dimension of the irreducible representation of SpS_{p} associated to the partition λ\lambda, with the condition that the length of the diagram λ\lambda is smaller than the dimension dd.

We now prove the claims about the convergence of the random variables λ1,2(d,s)\lambda_{1,2}^{(d,s)} from Section 3.

Proof of Proposition 3.4.

We start with the case where ss is fixed and we treat the λ1(d,s)\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)} random variable. We have

𝔼⁡[(λ1(d,s))p]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}\big)^{p}\Big] =s(s+1)⋯(s+p−1)∑β∈Spd#​βWgd​s(β)\displaystyle=s(s+1)\cdots(s+p-1)\sum_{\beta\in S_{p}}d^{\#\beta}{\operatorname{Wg}}_{ds}(\beta)
=s(s+1)⋯(s+p−1)∑β∈Spdp−|β|(ds)−p−|β|M​o¨​b(β)(1+O((ds)−2))\displaystyle=s(s+1)\cdots(s+p-1)\sum_{\beta\in S_{p}}d^{p-|\beta|}(ds)^{-p-|\beta|}\operatorname{M\ddot{o}b}(\beta)(1+O((ds)^{-2}))
=s−p⋅s(s+1)⋯(s+p−1)+O(d−1).\displaystyle=s^{-p}\cdot s(s+1)\cdots(s+p-1)+O(d^{-1}).

The assertion follows now from the observation that

s(s+1)⋯(s+p−1)=∫0∞xs+p−1(s−1)!e−xdxs(s+1)\cdots(s+p-1)=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{s+p-1}}{(s-1)!}e^{-x}\mathrm{d}x

is the pp-th moment of the Gamma distribution Γ⁡(s,1)\Gamma(s,1).

For the assertion regarding λ2(d,s)\lambda_{2}^{(d,s)}, compute

𝔼⁡[(λ2(d,s))p]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[(\lambda_{2}^{(d,s)})^{p}\right] =∑α,β∈Sps#​α​d#⁡(α​β)​Wgd​s⁡(α​β−1)\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}}s^{\#\alpha}d^{\#(\alpha\beta)}{\operatorname{Wg}}_{ds}(\alpha\beta^{-1})
=∑α,β∈Spsp−|α|​dp−|α​β|​(d​s)−p−|α​β−1|​(M​o¨​b⁡(α​β−1)+O⁡((d​s)−2))\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}}s^{p-|\alpha|}d^{p-|\alpha\beta|}(ds)^{-p-|\alpha\beta^{-1}|}(\operatorname{M\ddot{o}b}(\alpha\beta^{-1})+O((ds)^{-2}))
=∑α,β∈Sp|α​β|=|α​β−1|=0s−|α|+∑α,β∈Sp|α​β|+|α​β−1|=1s−|α|−|α​β−1|​d−1​M​o¨​b⁡(α​β−1)+O⁡(d−2)\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}\\ |\alpha\beta|=|\alpha\beta^{-1}|=0\end{subarray}}s^{-|\alpha|}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}\\ |\alpha\beta|+|\alpha\beta^{-1}|=1\end{subarray}}s^{-|\alpha|-|\alpha\beta^{-1}|}d^{-1}\operatorname{M\ddot{o}b}(\alpha\beta^{-1})+O(d^{-2})
=∑α∈Spα2=ids−|α|+∑α,β∈Sp|α​β|=1,|α​β−1|=0s−|α|​d−1−∑α,β∈Sp|α​β|=0,|α​β−1|=1s−|α|−1​d−1+O⁡(d−2)\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in S_{p}\\ \alpha^{2}=\mathrm{id}\end{subarray}}s^{-|\alpha|}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}\\ |\alpha\beta|=1,\,|\alpha\beta^{-1}|=0\end{subarray}}s^{-|\alpha|}d^{-1}-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}\\ |\alpha\beta|=0,\,|\alpha\beta^{-1}|=1\end{subarray}}s^{-|\alpha|-1}d^{-1}+O(d^{-2})
=∑α∈Spα2=ids−|α|+O⁡(d−2).\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in S_{p}\\ \alpha^{2}=\mathrm{id}\end{subarray}}s^{-|\alpha|}+O(d^{-2}).

Here we used the fact that there is no pair (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) such that |α​β|=1,|α​β−1|=0|\alpha\beta|=1,|\alpha\beta^{-1}|=0 or |α​β|=0,|α​β−1|=1|\alpha\beta|=0,|\alpha\beta^{-1}|=1. Indeed, for both two cases we have |α2|=1|\alpha^{2}|=1 or equivalently, α2\alpha^{2} is a transposition. However, this is impossible since sgn⁡(α2)=sgn​(α)2=1{\rm sgn}(\alpha^{2})={\rm sgn}(\alpha)^{2}=1. We have thus the moment limit

limd→∞𝔼⁡[(s​λ2(d,s))p]=∑π∈𝒫1,2​(p)s#​π,\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[(s\lambda_{2}^{(d,s)})^{p}]=\sum_{\pi\in\mathcal{P}_{1,2}(p)}s^{\#\pi},

where we have identified idempotent permutations α∈Sp\alpha\in S_{p} with partitions π=π⁡(α)∈𝒫⁡(p)\pi=\pi(\alpha)\in\mathcal{P}(p) having only blocks of size 11 or 22. Recall now that the normal distribution 𝒩⁡(s,s)\mathcal{N}(s,s) has classical cumulants

cn={s if n=1,2,0 otherwise.c_{n}=\begin{cases}s\quad\text{ if $n=1,2$,}\\ 0\quad\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

Hence the moment limit above corresponds to the pp-th moment of the normal distribution 𝒩⁡(s,s)\mathcal{N}(s,s) by the classical moment-cumulant formula, finishing the proof of the case ss fixed.

Let us now prove the statement (2) of the proposition, regarding the convergence λ1,2(d,s)→1\lambda_{1,2}^{(d,s)}\to 1 as d→∞d\to\infty and s⁡(d)→∞s(d)\to\infty. We start with the case of λ1(d,s)\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}. By Lemma A.11 and A.4, we have

𝔼⁡[(λ1(d,s))p]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[(\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)})^{p}\right] =sp​∑k=0∞ak,p​s−k​∑βdp−|β|​(d​s)−p−|β|​(M​o¨​b⁡(β)+O⁡((d​s)−2))\displaystyle=s^{p}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_{k,p}s^{-k}\sum_{\beta}d^{p-|\beta|}(ds)^{-p-|\beta|}(\operatorname{M\ddot{o}b}(\beta)+O((ds)^{-2}))
=∑k=0∞ak,p​s−k​(1−p⁡(p−1)2​d−2​s−1+O⁡((d​s)−2))\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_{k,p}s^{-k}\left(1-\frac{p(p-1)}{2}d^{-2}s^{-1}+O((ds)^{-2})\right)
=∑k=0∞ak,p​s−k+O⁡(d−2)\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_{k,p}s^{-k}+O(d^{-2})
=∑k=0N−1ak,p​s−k+O⁡(s−N)+O⁡(d−2)\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}a_{k,p}s^{-k}+O(s^{-N})+O(d^{-2})

for any integers p,N≥0p,N\geq 0. Then by Lemma A.3, we can further estimate

𝔼⁡[(λ1(d,s)−1)2​N]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[(\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}-1)^{2N}\right] =∑p=02​N(−1)2​N−p​𝔼​[(λ1(d,s))p]​(2​Np)\displaystyle=\sum_{p=0}^{2N}(-1)^{2N-p}\mathbb{E}[(\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)})^{p}]\binom{2N}{p}
=∑k=0N−1∑p=02​N(−1)2​N−p​ak,p​(2​Np)​s−k+O⁡(s−N)+O⁡(d−2)\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\sum_{p=0}^{2N}(-1)^{2N-p}a_{k,p}\binom{2N}{p}s^{-k}+O(s^{-N})+O(d^{-2})
=O⁡(s−N)+O⁡(d−2).\displaystyle=O(s^{-N})+O(d^{-2}).

In particular, this implies ‖λ1(d,s)−1‖L2​N→0\|\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}-1\|_{L^{2N}}\to 0 for all integers N≥1N\geq 1, and hence ‖λ1(d,s)−1‖Lp→0\|\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}-1\|_{L^{p}}\to 0 for all p∈(0,∞)p\in(0,\infty), whenever s,d→∞s,d\to\infty. Now assuming s≳dts\gtrsim d^{t} for some tt, we can choose NN such that N​t≥2Nt\geq 2 so that above estimation again implies

𝔼⁡[(λ1(d,s)−1)2​N]=O⁡(d−2).\mathbb{E}\left[(\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}-1)^{2N}\right]=O(d^{-2}).

Therefore, we have for any ε>0\varepsilon>0,

∑d=1∞ℙ⁡(|λ1(d,s)−1|≥ε)≤∑d=1∞𝔼⁡[(λ1(d,s)−1)2​N]ε2​N<∞\sum_{d=1}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}\left(|\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}-1|\geq\varepsilon\right)\leq\sum_{d=1}^{\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}[(\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}-1)^{2N}]}{\varepsilon^{2N}}<\infty

by the Markov inequality. Then the Borel-Cantelli lemma implies that λ1(d,s)→1\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}\to 1 almost surely.

The proof for λ2(d,s)\lambda_{2}^{(d,s)} is identical to the one above, up to replacing the constants ak,pa_{k,p} by the explicit constants bk,pb_{k,p} from Lemma A.4.

Finally, let us prove the statement (3) of Proposition 3.4. We show only the assertions for λ1(d,s)\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)} since the one for λ2(d,s)\lambda_{2}^{(d,s)} can be analogously shown. Lemma A.11 implies that for every ε>0\varepsilon>0,

ℙ(|d−tλ1(d,s)|>ε)≤1dN​t​εN𝔼[(λ1(d,s))N]=s1−p(s+1)⋯(s+N−1)O(d−N​t)=O(d−2),\mathbb{P}(|d^{-t}\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}|>\varepsilon)\leq\frac{1}{d^{Nt}\varepsilon^{N}}\mathbb{E}[(\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)})^{N}]=s^{1-p}(s+1)\cdots(s+N-1)O(d^{-Nt})=O(d^{-2}),

for any choice of large NN such that N​t≥2Nt\geq 2; this proves the claim in the regime d→∞d\to\infty. On the other hand, for the regime s→∞s\to\infty, Lemma A.11 again implies

𝔼⁡[(λ1(d,s))p]=1+p⁡(p−1)2​(1−d−2)​s−1+O⁡(s−2).\mathbb{E}[(\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)})^{p}]=1+\frac{p(p-1)}{2}(1-d^{-2})s^{-1}+O(s^{-2}).

Thus, we have

ℙ⁡(|d−t​(λ1(d,s)−1)|>ε)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(|d^{-t}(\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}-1)|>\varepsilon) ≤1d4​t​ε4​𝔼​[(λ1(d,s)−1)4]\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{d^{4t}\varepsilon^{4}}\mathbb{E}[(\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}-1)^{4}]
=∑p=04(−1)4−p​(1+p⁡(p−1)2​(1−d−2​s−1))+O⁡(s−2)=O⁡(s−2)\displaystyle=\sum_{p=0}^{4}(-1)^{4-p}\left(1+\frac{p(p-1)}{2}(1-d^{-2}s^{-1})\right)+O(s^{-2})=O(s^{-2})

by Lemma A.3. Now the usual Borel-Cantelli arguments again show the almost sure convergence d−t​(λ1(d,s)−1)→0d^{-t}(\lambda_{1}^{(d,s)}-1)\to 0 both for the cases d→∞d\to\infty and s→∞s\to\infty, and the proof is complete. ∎

We now show the convergence result for the random variable λ3(d,s)\lambda_{3}^{(d,s)}.

Proof of Proposition 4.3.

The proof proceeds by a moment computation using the formula for λ3(d,s)\lambda_{3}^{(d,s)} from Lemma A.11:

𝔼⁡[(λ3(d,s))p]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[(\lambda_{3}^{(d,s)})^{p}\right] =∑α,β∈Sps#​α​d#⁡(α∨β)​Wgd​s⁡(α​β−1)=1+∑α,β∈Sp(α,β)≠(id,id)s#​α​d#⁡(α∨β)​Wgd​s⁡(α​β−1)\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}}s^{\#\alpha}d^{\#(\alpha\vee\beta)}\operatorname{Wg}_{ds}(\alpha\beta^{-1})=1+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}\\ (\alpha,\beta)\neq(\mathrm{id},\mathrm{id})\end{subarray}}s^{\#\alpha}d^{\#(\alpha\vee\beta)}\operatorname{Wg}_{ds}(\alpha\beta^{-1})
=1+∑α,β∈Sp(α,β)≠(id,id)sp−|α|​dp−|α∨β|​(d​s)−p−|α​β−1|​(M​o¨​b⁡(α​β−1)+O⁡((d​s)−2))\displaystyle=1+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}\\ (\alpha,\beta)\neq(\mathrm{id},\mathrm{id})\end{subarray}}s^{p-|\alpha|}d^{p-|\alpha\vee\beta|}(ds)^{-p-|\alpha\beta^{-1}|}(\operatorname{M\ddot{o}b}(\alpha\beta^{-1})+O((ds)^{-2}))
=1+∑α,β∈Sp(α,β)≠(id,id)|α∨β|+|α​β−1|=1s−|α|−|α​β−1|​d−1​M​o¨​b⁡(α​β−1)+O⁡(d−2)\displaystyle=1+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}\\ (\alpha,\beta)\neq(\mathrm{id},\mathrm{id})\\ |\alpha\vee\beta|+|\alpha\beta^{-1}|=1\end{subarray}}s^{-|\alpha|-|\alpha\beta^{-1}|}d^{-1}\operatorname{M\ddot{o}b}(\alpha\beta^{-1})+O(d^{-2})
=1+∑α,β∈Sp(α,β)≠(id,id)|α∨β|=1,|α​β−1|=0s−|α|​d−1+O⁡(d−2)\displaystyle=1+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}\\ (\alpha,\beta)\neq(\mathrm{id},\mathrm{id})\\ |\alpha\vee\beta|=1,\,|\alpha\beta^{-1}|=0\end{subarray}}s^{-|\alpha|}d^{-1}+O(d^{-2})
=1+p⁡(p−1)2​(d​s)−1+O⁡(d−2).\displaystyle=1+\frac{p(p-1)}{2}(ds)^{-1}+O(d^{-2}).

Using Lemma A.3, we can show

𝔼⁡[(λ3(d,s)−1)4]=O⁡(d−2).\mathbb{E}\left[(\lambda_{3}^{(d,s)}-1)^{4}\right]=O(d^{-2}).

The almost sure convergence λ3(d,s)→1\lambda_{3}^{(d,s)}\to 1 follows by the Markov inequality and the Borel-Cantelli lemma. ∎

A.3. Matrix parameters

This section contains results about the matrix parameters A,B,CA,B,C which appear in the study of random CDUC, DUC, and DOC quantum channels from Section 5.

We begin with the description of average moments. Note that for our analysis, only the asymptotic eigenvalue distribution and moments of the matrix CC is needed. We give, for the sake of completeness, the formulas for the three matrices.

Lemma A.12.

The average ppth moment of the random matrices A,B,CA,B,C are given by

𝔼⁡[Tr⁡(Ap)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\Tr(A^p)] =∑α,β∈Sps#​α​d#⁡((γ−1​α​γ)∨β)​Wgd​s​(α​β−1),\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}}s^{\#\alpha}d^{\#((\gamma^{-1}\alpha\gamma)\vee\beta)}{\rm Wg}_{ds}(\alpha\beta^{-1}),
𝔼⁡[Tr⁡(Bp)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\Tr(B^p)] =∑α,β∈Sps#​α​d#⁡((γ−1​α)∨(γ−1​β))​Wgd​s​(α​β−1),\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}}s^{\#\alpha}d^{\#((\gamma^{-1}\alpha)\vee(\gamma^{-1}\beta))}{\rm Wg}_{ds}(\alpha\beta^{-1}),
𝔼⁡[Tr⁡(Cp)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\Tr(C^p)] =∑α,β∈Sps#​α​d#⁡((γ−1​α)∨(γ−1​β−1))​Wgd​s​(α​β−1),\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}}s^{\#\alpha}d^{\#((\gamma^{-1}\alpha)\vee(\gamma^{-1}\beta^{-1}))}{\rm Wg}_{ds}(\alpha\beta^{-1}),

where γ=(pp−1⋯ 2 1)∈Sp\gamma=(p\;p-1\;\cdots\;2\;1)\in S_{p} is the full cycle.

Proof.

We shall prove the result only for the matrix CC, since it is the only result we shall use later. The proofs for A,BA,B are similar and we leave them to the reader.

To show the third formula above, we need to compute the expectation of the diagram in Fig. 10, which is obtained by tracing the product of pp copies of the diagram for CC from Fig. 8.

To compute the expectation value of the diagram, we use the graphical Weingarten formula from [CN10, CN15]. We obtain a sum indexed by a pair of permutations α,β∈Sp\alpha,\beta\in S_{p} of diagrams 𝒟α,β\mathcal{D}_{\alpha,\beta}, weighted by the Weingarten function Wgd​s⁡(α​β−1)\operatorname{Wg}_{ds}(\alpha\beta^{-1}). Each diagram 𝒟α,β\mathcal{D}_{\alpha,\beta} in the sum will be a collection of loops corresponding to the ℂd\mathbb{C}^{d} and ℂs\mathbb{C}^{s} vector spaces. Our goal is to count how many loops of each type appear in the diagram 𝒟α,β\mathcal{D}_{\alpha,\beta}. We refer to Fig. 11 for the construction of the diagram 𝒟α,β\mathcal{D}_{\alpha,\beta}, obtained by erasing the VV and the V∗V^{*} boxes, and connecting the loose wires using α\alpha for the left side of the VV boxes and β\beta for the right side of the VV boxes. Note that in the Weingarten formula (21), the indices of VV and V¯\overline{V} are matched; in our setting, we connect to the opposite sides of V∗=V¯⊤V^{*}=\overline{V}^{\top}.

The number of loops of type ss in 𝒟α,β\mathcal{D}_{\alpha,\beta} is easily computed: only the permutation α\alpha is involved in connecting the ss-type wires, and it is easy to see that each cycle of α\alpha yields a connected component (loop) in the end. We have thus a contribution of s#​αs^{\#\alpha}. The computation of the loops of size dd is more complicated, because of the presence of the “vertical” connection between the ii-th VV and V∗V^{*} boxes. In the absence of this vertical connection, each VV box would have been connected to the previous V∗V^{*} box, resulting in a total number of #⁡(γ−1​α)+#⁡(γ−1​β−1)\#(\gamma^{-1}\alpha)+\#(\gamma^{-1}\beta^{-1}) dd-loops. The vertical wire connects some of the resulting loops, yielding the announced number of connected components (loops). ∎

Let us now consider the matrix elements of the three parameters A,B,CA,B,C. We first compute the moments.

Lemma A.13.

For i,ji,j, the ppth moment of the entry Ai​jA_{ij} is

𝔼⁡[(Ai​j)p]=s(s+1)⋯(s+p−1)ds(ds+1)⋯(ds+p−1).\mathbb{E}\left[(A_{ij})^{p}\right]=\frac{s(s+1)\cdots(s+p-1)}{ds(ds+1)\cdots(ds+p-1)}.

Moreover, for i≠ji\neq j, the ppth moment of the values |Bi​j|2|B_{ij}|^{2} and |Ci​j|2|C_{ij}|^{2} are

𝔼[|Bi​j|2​p]=𝔼[|Ci​j|2​p]=p!s(s+1)⋯(s+p−1)∑β∈𝒮Wgd​s(β),\mathbb{E}\left[|B_{ij}|^{2p}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[|C_{ij}|^{2p}\right]=p!s(s+1)\cdots(s+p-1)\sum_{\beta\in\mathcal{S}}{\rm Wg}_{ds}(\beta),

where 𝒮={α∈S2​p:α⁡(i)≡i​mod​ 2​ for all ​i}\mathcal{S}=\set{\alpha\in S_{2p}:\alpha(i)\equiv i\;{\rm mod}\,2\text{ for all }i}. In particular, |Bi​j||B_{ij}| and |Ci​j||C_{ij}| have the same distribution.

Proof.

(Figure 12) By Weingarten calculus and Lemma A.2, we have

𝔼⁡[(Ai​j)p]=∑α,β∈Sps#​α​Wgd​s​(α​β−1)=∑α∈Sps#​α​∑β∈SpWgd​s​(β)=s(s+1)⋯(s+p−1)ds(ds+1)⋯(ds+p−1).\mathbb{E}\left[(A_{ij})^{p}\right]=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in S_{p}}s^{\#\alpha}{\rm Wg}_{ds}(\alpha\beta^{-1})=\sum_{\alpha\in S_{p}}s^{\#\alpha}\sum_{\beta\in S_{p}}{\rm Wg}_{ds}(\beta)=\frac{s(s+1)\cdots(s+p-1)}{ds(ds+1)\cdots(ds+p-1)}.

Next, since Bi​j=Bj​i¯B_{ij}=\overline{B_{ji}}, we have

where 𝒯={α∈S2​p:α⁡(i)≡i+1​mod​ 2​ for all ​i}\mathcal{T}=\set{\alpha\in S_{2p}:\alpha(i)\equiv i+1\;{\rm mod}\,2\text{ for all }i}. Note the the last equality follows from the observation that for any α∈𝒯\alpha\in\mathcal{T}, the map β∈𝒯↦α​β−1∈𝒮\beta\in\mathcal{T}\mapsto\alpha\beta^{-1}\in\mathcal{S} is a bijection. We claim that the map

φ:α∈𝒯↦α2|{1,3,…,2​p−1}∈S⁡({1,3,…,2​p−1})\varphi:\alpha\in\mathcal{T}\mapsto\alpha^{2}\big|_{\{1,3,\ldots,2p-1\}}\in S(\{1,3,\ldots,2p-1\})

is well-defined p!p!-to-11 surjection and #⁡(φ⁡(α))=#​α\#(\varphi(\alpha))=\#\alpha. ασ,π​(2​i−1)=π⁡(2​i−1),ασ,π​(π⁡(2​i−1))=σ⁡(2​i−1)\alpha_{\sigma,\pi}(2i-1)=\pi(2i-1),\quad\alpha_{\sigma,\pi}(\pi(2i-1))=\sigma(2i-1)

so that φ⁡(ασ,π)=σ\varphi(\alpha_{\sigma,\pi})=\sigma. One can easily check

and #⁡(ασ,π)=#​σ\#(\alpha_{\sigma,\pi})=\#\sigma regardless of the choice of π\pi, and therefore the claim is shown. Now from the claim and Lemma A.2, we obtain that

∑α∈𝒯s#​α=∑α∈𝒯s#​φ​(α)=p!∑σ∈Sps#​σ=p!s(s+1)⋯(s+p−1),\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal{T}}s^{\#\alpha}=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal{T}}s^{\#\varphi(\alpha)}=p!\sum_{\sigma\in S_{p}}s^{\#\sigma}=p!s(s+1)\cdots(s+p-1),

hence proving the moment formula 𝔼⁡[|Bi​j|2​p]\mathbb{E}[|B_{ij}|^{2p}].

The moment 𝔼⁡[|Ci​j|2​p]\mathbb{E}[|C_{ij}|^{2p}] is calculated by the same method. These moments satisfy Carleman’s condition [Akh20, Chapter 2, Addenda and Problems, 11], so the distributions of |Bi​j||B_{ij}| and |Ci​j||C_{ij}| are the same by uniqueness of the moments. ∎

This allows us to prove the limit result for the entries of A,B,CA,B,C.

Proof of Proposition 5.8.

(1) and (2) is clear from

limd→∞𝔼⁡[(d​s​Ai​j)p]\displaystyle\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[(dsA_{ij})^{p}] =limd→∞(ds)ps(s+1)⋯(s+p−1)ds(ds+1)⋯(ds+p−1)=s(s+1)⋯(s+p−1),\displaystyle=\lim_{d\to\infty}\frac{(ds)^{p}s(s+1)\cdots(s+p-1)}{ds(ds+1)\cdots(ds+p-1)}=s(s+1)\cdots(s+p-1),
limd→∞𝔼⁡[|d​s​Bi​j|2​p]=limd→∞𝔼⁡[|d​s​Ci​j|2​p]\displaystyle\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[|dsB_{ij}|^{2p}]=\lim_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[|dsC_{ij}|^{2p}] =limd→∞p!(ds)ps(s+1)⋯(s+p−1)(ds)−p(1+O((ds)−1))\displaystyle=\lim_{d\to\infty}p!(ds)^{p}s(s+1)\cdots(s+p-1)(ds)^{-p}(1+O((ds)^{-1}))
=p!s(s+1)⋯(s+p−1),\displaystyle=p!s(s+1)\cdots(s+p-1),

by Lemma A.13, and the fact that s(s+1)⋯(s+p−1)s(s+1)\cdots(s+p-1) and p!p! are pp-th moment of the Gamma distribution Γ⁡(s,1)\Gamma(s,1) and the exponential distribution 𝖤𝗑𝗉⁡(1)\mathsf{Exp}(1), as noted in the proof of Proposition 3.4.

For the proof of (3), let us recall from Eq. 16 that the random variables

Ain​jn=∑k=1s|Vin​jn(k)|2,Ajn​in=∑k=1s|Vin​jn(k)|2,Bin​jn=∑k=1sVin​in(k)​Vjn​jn(k)¯,A_{i_{n}j_{n}}=\sum_{k=1}^{s}|V_{i_{n}j_{n}}^{(k)}|^{2},\quad A_{j_{n}i_{n}}=\sum_{k=1}^{s}|V_{i_{n}j_{n}}^{(k)}|^{2},\quad B_{i_{n}j_{n}}=\sum_{k=1}^{s}V_{i_{n}i_{n}}^{(k)}\overline{V_{j_{n}j_{n}}^{(k)}},

for n=1,…,Nn=1,\ldots,N, are functions of the 2​s×2​N2s\times 2N-submatrix V(2​s×2​N)V^{(2s\times 2N)} of VV, where V(2​s×2​N)V^{(2s\times 2N)} can be written as a block matrix (Vi1​j1(2​s×2)Vi2​j2(2​s×2)⋯ViN​jN(2​s×2))\left(V_{i_{1}j_{1}}^{(2s\times 2)}\;V_{i_{2}j_{2}}^{(2s\times 2)}\;\cdots\;V_{i_{N}j_{N}}^{(2s\times 2)}\right) for

Vi​j(2​s×2):=(Vi​i(1)Vi​j(1)Vi​i(s)Vi​j(s)Vj​i(1)Vj​j(1)Vj​i(s)Vj​j(s)).V_{ij}^{(2s\times 2)}:=\begin{pmatrix}V_{ii}^{(1)}&V_{ij}^{(1)}\\ \vdots&\vdots\\ V_{ii}^{(s)}&V_{ij}^{(s)}\\ V_{ji}^{(1)}&V_{jj}^{(1)}\\ \vdots&\vdots\\ V_{ji}^{(s)}&V_{jj}^{(s)}\end{pmatrix}.

However, it is known [PR04, MT07] that if ss and NN are fixed, the random matrix d​s​V(2​s×2​N)\sqrt{ds}V^{(2s\times 2N)} converges in distribution to the (2​s×2​N)(2s\times 2N) Ginibre ensemble whose entries are standard normal random variable as d→∞d\to\infty. In particular, the entries of d​s​V(2​s×2​N)\sqrt{ds}V^{(2s\times 2N)} are asymptotically independent. Now the assertion follows from the observation that all the summands defining {Ain​jn,Ajn​in,Bin​jn}n=1N\{A_{i_{n}j_{n}},A_{j_{n}i_{n}},B_{i_{n}j_{n}}\}_{n=1}^{N} are distinct. ∎

Proof of Proposition 5.9.

=(∑k=0∞ak,p​s−k)​(1+∑k=1∞ak,p​(d​s)−k)−1\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_{k,p}s^{-k}\right)\left(1+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}a_{k,p}(ds)^{-k}\right)^{-1}
